title: Assessing diversified farming’s effects on Central American cacao and coffee smallholders’ food security and vulnerability
abstract: Diversified farming is one of several agroecological strategies for reducing smallholders’ risk and building resilience to climate change and other hazards. Accumulating evidence shows that farmers can use agroecology to improve household food security and influence food system transformations. However, additional research is needed to identify which agroecological strategies are used by whom and to what degree diversification, household characteristics, context, or other strategies contribute to farmer well-being and resilience. In 2022, we conducted a livelihood, agriculture, and food security survey with 429 randomly sampled smallholders, including 309 coffee farmers in northern Nicaragua’s Segovias region and 120 cacao farmers in north-central Nicaragua’s Waslala region. We examined the relationships linking diversified production—and other key agroecological principles—to food security, water security, and dietary diversity. We integrated statistical analysis into our participatory mixed methods approach using partner feedback to help design the survey and 13 farmer interviews to inform and interpret the statistical models. We found that cacao farmers in the wetter growing zone reported more crop diversity and organic production and less seasonal hunger than coffee growers. Food and input price inflation were more pressing concerns than the impact of hurricanes Eta and Iota for all producers. Our multivariate analysis found that significant correlates of food security included surplus subsistence (corn and bean) production, water security, farm size, and income. Product diversity and farmers’ formal education correlated significantly with household dietary diversity. This study finds evidence that agroecological diversified farming can enhance food security and dietary diversity among coffee and cacao smallholders. This is among the first studies comparing how cacao and coffee farmers’ diversified and agroecological production strategies relate to food security, water security, nutrition, and vulnerability, potentially holding implications for the 15 million plus smallholder coffee and cacao growers seeking more sustainable livelihoods and landscapes.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Mechanical Engineering: Foundations, Opportunities, Challenges, and Responsibilities
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mechanical engineering (ME), from modeling, simulation, and optimization to diagnostics, design, and technical communication. Drawing on a round-table at the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering (COBEM 2025), this article presents a structured perspective for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than an exhaustive survey, it examines how AI can enhance engineering practice without compromising scientific rigor. We distinguish statistical learning from human cognition and discuss the capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic forms of AI. We then consider industrial adoption, workforce changes, and AI-assisted scientific discovery, alongside the energy and infrastructure demands of AI computation and their implications for sustainability and thermal management. The discussion emphasizes the integration of physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems, particularly in safety-relevant applications. Topics include physics-informed and hybrid learning, physically constrained modeling, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification. We also examine educational, epistemological, and ethical challenges, including curriculum reform, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the preservation of engineering knowledge. We conclude with principles for responsible AI adoption in ME: physical consistency, rigorous validation, explicit treatment of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. AI should complement, not replace, engineering judgment.

title: A psychological prediction automatic reasoning framework for explaining potential cognitive states
abstract: Psychological prediction, the ability to infer human behavior and intentions, is essential for artificial intelligence and human–machine interaction. Existing deep learning models often rely on surface-level fitting and lack structured abductive interpretability, while traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from non-differentiable discontinuities and limited adaptability to dynamic contextual constraints. This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic automated reasoning framework for modeling latent cognitive states under contextual constraints. The framework introduces a context-aware adaptive SMC resampling operator (CAR-SMC), which uses energy-based penalties to filter hypotheses violating contextual constraints. We further design an executable differentiable program synthesis (EDPS) module and a hybrid iterative program–cognition interaction (HIPCI) mechanism. Through stop-gradient-based directional optimization, HIPCI separates the update pathways of belief and program representations during alternating fixed-point optimization, reducing circular gradient entanglement. Experiments on OpenToM and FANToM show that the framework improves the abductive consistency rate (ACR), an empirical belief–action consistency metric, to 70.8% and 52.1%, respectively. Under the adopted classification-oriented evaluation setup, these results indicate additional ACR gains over pure fine-tuned encoder classifiers and higher ACR than the evaluated few-shot ToT reference baseline (~ 7B), while using fewer parameters and maintaining an average inference latency of 215 ms per instance. Overall, this work provides a differentiable framework for machine Theory of Mind with process-level structural interpretability under the evaluated text-based classification setting.

title: Novel index on the propensity for digital transformation in agriculture (PADiTIndex)
abstract: Digital agriculture is one of the levers that will enable food systems to adapt and remain resilient in the face of climate change. However, in addition to being generally slow to take off, its adoption is not geographically uniform. While studies at the producer level have investigated the rationale for this disparity, we argue that it could be that different countries and markets are prepared to absorb digital technologies into their value chains. This study assesses the propensity of different countries and markets to digitally transform their agriculture using a new proposed index named Propensity for Agricultural Digital Transformation Index (PADiTIndex) . It uses four indicators including the economic weight of agriculture in the country’s economy, the vulnerability/resilience of the country’s agricultural sector to climate change, the country’s agricultural productivity, and its openness to innovation. To this end, time series data for these four indicators were collected from FAOSTAT, ND- GAIN, USDA and WDCR for the period 2015–2022, making the assessment scalable. A few cases of missing data were completed by interpolation while normalization was used to transform the four indicators that were in different units into a single comparable format. The results indicate that the value of agricultural production per agricultural worker, the resilience of food systems to climate change, and national openness to innovation are the country-level dimensions most closely associated with the propensity of economies to digitally transform their agriculture. In this regard, the Netherlands, Israel, Belgium, Denmark, and Luxembourg stand out as the top five countries where the digital transformation of agriculture is most evident. Conversely, the five countries with the lowest rankings are in Africa (Niger, Madagascar, Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, and Guinea), suggesting room for improvement, beginning with fostering a stronger commitment to modernizing their agricultural sectors to enhance their resilience. This work also corroborates findings from studies, highlighting the well-documented importance of socioeconomic factors in climate change adaptation planning.

title: Machine Learning Model Using Clinical and Contrast-Enhanced MRI Features Differentiates Cerebral Tuberculoma from Lung Cancer Brain Metastasis.
abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES Cerebral tuberculomas (CTB) and lung cancer brain metastases (BM) frequently show overlapping appearances on conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) but require entirely different treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model integrating clinical and contrast-enhanced MRI features to noninvasively differentiate these two entities. MATERIALS AND METHODS The internal dataset (n = 188, 122 CTB, 66 BM) was split into training/validation (n = 131) and internal test (n = 57) sets. Feature selection (univariate and stepwise logistic regression) was performed only on the training and validation set, yielding four predictors. Machine learning classifiers were trained using these predictors with repeated 5-fold cross-validation. An external test set (n = 51, 26 CTB, 25 BM) from another hospital was used for independent validation. RESULTS Multivariate logistic regression retained four independent predictors: age (OR = 1.046, 95%CI: 1.003-1.091, p = 0.036), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (odds ratios [OR] = 1.711, 95%confidence intervals [CI]: 1.235-2.370, p = 0.001), multiple lesions (OR = 0.080, 95%CI: 0.015-0.438, p = 0.004), and ring with mural nodule (OR = 11.289, 95%CI: 2.551-49.952, p = 0.001). The Gradient Boosting model built on these four features achieved the best performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.970 (95%CI: 0.925-0.998) on the internal test set and 0.957 (95%CI: 0.900-0.995) on the external test set. On the external test set, the model showed a sensitivity of 88.0% and a specificity of 92.3%. CONCLUSION A Gradient Boosting model integrating age, CEA, multiple lesions, and ring with mural nodule effectively distinguishes CTB from BM with robust external test performance, providing a noninvasive tool to assist clinical decision-making.

Chitosan-functionalized Ajuga integrifolia-mediated zinc oxide nanoparticles for antidiabetic and anti-inflammatory applications: An integrated In Vitro, In Vivo, and In Silico study.
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by high blood glucose levels (BGL), while inflammation is an adaptive physiological response which is triggered by adverse conditions, including infection and tissue damage. In the present study, Ajuga integrifolia (AI) mediated zinc oxide nanoparticles (AI-ZnO NPs) were prepared and functionalized with chitosan (CS). The synthesized AI-ZnO and CS-ZnO NPs were characterized using advanced techniques. UV-Visible spectroscopic analysis showed a prominent peak of AI-ZnO at 361 nm, which blue-shifted to 347 nm with CS coating. Functional groups were identified using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), while particle morphology and size were characterized using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). X-ray Diffraction (XRD) confirmed the hexagonal wurtzite structure. Laminin, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), Islet Amyloid Polypeptide (IAPP), and alpha-glucosidase were docked with chitosan, yielding distinct binding energies as well as varying interaction residues, interaction types, and distances. The in vitro antidiabetic and anti-inflammatory assays showed considerable potential, with inhibition ranging from 12.1 ± 2.01% to 89.46 ± 0.77%. The in vivo antidiabetic and anti-inflammatory experiments were performed in a murine model. BGL increased markedly from the normal baseline (95 mg/dl) to about 224 mg/dl within 24 h of alloxan administration. 40 mg/kg of CS-ZnO showed the highest potential, lowering the BGL to 121 ± 2 mg/dl. The ear edema decreased from 0.35 mm to 0.26 mm with 40 mg/kg of CS-ZnO. The histopathological images also confirmed the medicinal potential of the test samples, which may serve as alternative medicinal agents in the future.

Vision Transformers for Estimating Irradiance Using Data Scarce Sky Images
abstract: Accurate estimation of diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) is critical for optimising photovoltaic system performance and energy forecasting yet remains challenging in regions lacking comprehensive ground-based instrumentation. Recent advancements using Vision Transformers (ViTs) trained on extensive sky image datasets have shown promise in replacing costly irradiance measurement equipment, but the scarcity of long-term, high-quality sky imagery significantly restricts practical implementation. Addressing this critical gap, this study proposes a novel dual-framework approach designed for data-scarce scenarios. First, calculated atmospheric parameters, including extraterrestrial irradiance and cyclic time encodings, are integrated to represent sky conditions without utilising any instrumentation. Next, a sequential pipeline initially predicts synthetic global horizontal irradiance (GHI) and uses it as a feature, to refine DHI estimation. Finally, a dual-parallel architecture simultaneously processes raw and overlay-enhanced fisheye sky images. Overlays are generated through unsupervised, physics-informed cloud segmentation to highlight dynamic sky features. Empirical validation is performed using data from the Chilbolton Observatory, chosen for its temperate climate and frequent cloud variability. To simulate data-scarce conditions, models are trained on a single month (e.g., January) and evaluated across a temporally disjoint, full-year test set. Under this setup, the sequential and dual-parallel frameworks achieve RMSE values within 2-3 W/m^2 and 1-6 W/m^2, respectively, of a state-of-the-art ViT trained on the complete dataset. By combining physics-informed modelling with unsupervised segmentation, the proposed method provides a scalable and cost-effective solution for DHI estimation, advancing solar resource assessment in data-constrained environments.

title: One-shot federated unsupervised domain adaptation with Smoothed Knowledge Distillation and teacher refinement
abstract: Federated unsupervised domain adaptation (FUDA) addresses the challenge of adapting models to an unlabeled target domain using decentralized source domains while preserving data privacy. However, existing FUDA methods typically require multiple communication rounds, rely on complex aggregation strategies, and often struggle with noisy pseudo labels and inconsistent source knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose SKD-ETR, a novel one-shot FUDA framework that combines Smoothed Knowledge Distillation (SKD) and Exponential moving average-based Teacher Refinement (ETR). SKD trains a student model on the target domain using smoothed soft pseudo labels generated by the ensemble of source models. This reduces overconfidence, mitigates noise, and improves robustness. ETR further refines each source model by interpolating its parameters toward the student via exponential moving average (EMA), thereby transferring target-domain knowledge back to the teachers. This bidirectional refinement enhances pseudo-label quality and student generalization without additional communication overhead. SKD-ETR eliminates complex aggregation by initializing the student model randomly and performing a single-round distillation process. Extensive experiments on OfficeHome, Office-Caltech, and DomainNet demonstrate that SKD-ETR achieves competitive performance while being communication- and computation-efficient, and robust under noisy supervision. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/A-Abedi/SKD_ETR.

title: Humanity in the loop: Reframing artificial intelligence and the global medical imaging divide.
abstract: OBJECTIVES Access to radiology and nuclear medicine remains profoundly unequal across global health systems. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face persistent shortages in imaging equipment, specialist workforce, digital infrastructure, maintenance, regulation and sustainable financing. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism to improve imaging access, but it may also reinforce existing inequities. This narrative review examines the potential for discriminative, generative and agentic AI to reduce or widen inequities in LMIC medical imaging and proposes a sociotechnical governance framework based on the concept of Humanity-in-the-Loop. KEY FINDINGS Discriminative AI may improve image interpretation, triage, segmentation, quantification and image-quality assessment; generative AI may enhance reporting, education, translation, communication, synthetic data generation and research workflows; and agentic AI may coordinate referrals, scheduling, follow-up, supply logistics and imaging pathways. They may also exacerbate inequity through data colonialism, algorithmic under-performance, dataset shift, infrastructure dependence, commercial lock-in, second-tier automation, liability transfer and unequal participation in AI research and development. CONCLUSION Human-in-the-loop governance is insufficient for equitable AI implementation in LMIC medical imaging because the assumptions underpinning effective human oversight are often absent in resource-constrained settings. The proposed Humanity-in-the-Loop sociotechnical framework embeds equity, local agency, contextual validity and public benefit throughout the AI lifecycle. The framework comprises six interconnected domains: patient humanity, workforce humanity, community humanity, data humanity, system humanity and global humanity. IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE Responsible implementation of AI in medical imaging requires governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithm performance to include workforce development, data sovereignty, infrastructure, community priorities, equitable partnerships and sustainable capacity building. Adoption of a Humanity-in-the-Loop approach may help ensure that AI narrows rather than widens the medical imaging divide between high-income countries and LMICs.

title: Synthetic activation of gibberellin signalling reveals spatial coordination of root growth.
Fine-scale characterization of dispersed-village landscapes: data challenges and methodological advances for rural landscape mapping and assessment in Pomerania, Poland
abstract: Dispersed-village landscapes in Pomerania are shaped by local environmental conditions and long-term farming practices, yet standard spatial datasets generalize many fine-scale landscape elements. In this pilot study, we developed and tested a fine-scale mapping and assessment approach at the 64-ha Knyki-1 reference site using a custom 3-level land-use/land-cover (LULC) scheme, an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-derived digital surface model (DSM), field mapping, plant-cover inventories, and GIS analysis. We compared custom mapping with CORINE Land Cover (CLC) and the Topographic Objects Database (BDOT10k) using landscape- and class-level metrics. At the Knyki-1 site, standard datasets strongly generalized or omitted small patches, linear elements, woody structures, and structural transition zones that may correspond to ecotonal structures. The custom mapping represented 21 LULC classes and 148 patches, versus 2–6 classes and 6–28 patches in the standard datasets, showing how dataset choice affects landscape representation and structural inference. Field inventories documented ancient-forest indicators, archaeophytes, and protected vascular-plant taxa across multiple landscape components. The resulting fine-scale baseline may support future repeated monitoring and, after multi-site validation, regional landscape assessment, conservation planning, and management. These natural–cultural rural landscapes remain absent from national landscape classifications and are increasingly vulnerable to pressures from the abandonment of traditional agriculture.

title: Conflict with industrial fleets undermines the contributions of small-scale fisheries to sustainable development in vulnerable regions
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract: Equitable and sustainable governance of small-scale fisheries (SSFs) is essential for achieving food security and conservation in coastal areas. Yet in increasingly industrialized oceans, competition and conflict with large-scale fisheries (LSFs) threaten the contributions of SSFs to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Here we have developed a small-scale and industrial fisheries interaction index and applied it to 126 countries using 2 recent global datasets. Vulnerability to conflict is highest in countries where SSFs are vital for nutrition, but governance is weak, especially in Africa, Oceania and Asia. We also identify low-exposure outlier countries with unexpectedly low risk of SSF–LSF interactions, providing insights for proactive policy. Preferential access areas granting spatial rights to SSFs are common in both low- and high-vulnerability countries, suggesting such policies are often reactive and may be insufficient alone without strong enforcement. As ocean industries expand, it will be necessary to strengthen SSF access rights and limit LSF overcapacity to reduce conflict and advance sustainable development. Small-scale fisheries are vulnerable to conflict with industrial fishing. The small-scale and industrial fisheries interaction index reveals regions with weak governance and emphasizes the need for enhanced access rights and management strategies.

title: The global potential of aquavoltaics for power generation and offsetting the carbon footprint of freshwater aquaculture
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract: Global inland freshwater aquaculture has rapidly expanded, intensifying greenhouse gas emissions and sustainability challenges. Here we estimate whether aquavoltaics, integrating photovoltaics with aquaculture, could offer multifunctional benefits. We integrate satellite observation products with realistic climate-driven photovoltaic system simulations to map the global expansion patterns and installation potential of aquavoltaics. Global aquavoltaics area covered 423 km2 in 2023, with China accounting for the overwhelming majority (97%). We estimate that deploying photovoltaics with a 40% coverage rate across over 50,000 km2 of landside clustering of aquaculture ponds globally could yield an electricity generation potential of 4,143 ± 145 TWh yr-1. Aquavoltaics deployment could support energy self-sufficiency in 878 cities and offset the freshwater aquaculture carbon footprint in 61 countries through grid-level avoided emissions. These findings highlight aquavoltaics as a scalable pathway within the energy-food-climate nexus to support sustainable aquaculture and low-carbon energy futures alongside aquatic food production.

Long-term effects of crop rotation and nitrogen management on nitrous oxide emissions in agricultural systems: a narrative review
abstract: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 265 to 298 times that of carbon dioxide over a century, and the principal anthropogenic stratospheric ozone-depleting substance now emitted to the atmosphere. Agricultural soils account for roughly 60% of anthropogenic emissions, so cropping sequence and nitrogen inputs directly shape emission rates. Drawing on 18 long-term field studies spanning 5 to 45 years and twelve countries, this review examines how crop rotation, tillage, organic and synthetic nitrogen fertilisation, and their interactions with soil and climate govern N2O across multi-decadal timescales. Management effects are rarely consistent across sites: no-till reduces emissions in well-drained temperate soils but raises them in waterlogged fine-textured soils, and organic fertilisers lower emissions when mineralisation matches crop uptake but raise them when labile carbon and nitrogen accumulate together. Mean N2O rises with temperature across studies, implying that warming will amplify emissions most in under-monitored tropical regions. The review identifies geographic gaps, inconsistent flux protocols, and weak integration of microbial ecology and process modelling as the main barriers to transferable guidance. Its contribution is a mechanistically grounded, management-organised synthesis that moves beyond aggregate effect sizes and proposes a research agenda for climate-smart nitrogen governance. This review is timely: as reactive-nitrogen use and global warming intensify together, and with N2O now the principal anthropogenic ozone-depleting substance emitted, it offers researchers, greenhouse-gas-inventory compilers and policymakers a transferable, mechanistically grounded basis for emission-reduction guidance across the diverse soils and climates where food is produced.

title: Probabilistic Response of Prestressed Concrete Box Girder Bridges under Stochastic Temperature–Humidity Environmental Conditions
abstract: To investigate the evolution of mechanical behavior in concrete box girder bridges during cantilever construction under the coupled influence of stochastic environmental temperature and humidity, a novel simulation method is proposed. This method integrates a temperature–humidity coupling analysis method for the internal fields of concrete and a constitutive model that accounts for multifactor interactions, including temperature-induced stress, drying shrinkage, creep, and the sensitivity of elastic modulus. The proposed method was applied to simulate and analyze the construction process of the Yuanhe Bridge in Jiangxi Province, China. Based on the statistical analysis of nearly two decades of daily historical meteorological data from the region, it was verified through fitting tests and statistical assessments that the probability distributions of temperature, humidity, and wind speed conform to Gaussian (normal) distributions. The results systematically reveal the statistical influences of stochastic environmental factors on the bridge’s camber, shear-lag effect, and prestress loss. The results indicate that the maximum camber and the shear-lag coefficient at the bottom slab–web junction exhibit slightly asymmetric distributions and can be well described by Bigaussian fitting curves, whereas the shear-lag coefficient at the top slab–web junction follows a Gaussian distribution. Increases in the daily temperature range and decreases in relative humidity are found to amplify the camber and the prestress loss. No discernible influence of wind speed on the camber, shear-lag effect, or prestress loss is observed. This study provides a crucial theoretical foundation and technical support for the refined control and optimization of cantilever construction of bridges under stochastic environmental conditions.

title: Replacing blanket agronomic recommendations with agroecology-specific decision support: a simulation-based framework for irrigated dry-season rice production in coastal deltas
abstract: Irrigated dry-season (Boro) rice (Oryza sativa L.) is a major contributor to food security in Bangladesh and inland West Bengal, but its cultivation is limited in the coastal Sundarbans due to high salinity, tidal influences, and scarcity of fresh irrigation water. Current policy frameworks promoting uniform transplanting windows and cultivar choices disregard the marked spatial heterogeneity of abiotic stress regimes in these deltaic agroecosystems. This study aimed to characterize genotype × environment × management (G × E × M) interactions and identify location-specific sowing date–cultivar combinations to improve Boro rice productivity, irrigation water productivity, and yield stability under coastal saline conditions. The Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM-Oryza) was calibrated and validated using multi-location field experimental data from Bangladesh and India collected during 2016–2018. Model performance was evaluated for phenology, above-ground biomass, and grain yield, with root mean square errors (RMSEs) of 6.7 days, 996 kg ha−1, and 1574 kg ha−1, respectively. Subsequently, 35 years of climate-driven simulations (1984–2018) were conducted to assess the effects of sowing dates and cultivar choices on crop performance, stress exposure, irrigation requirements, and irrigation water productivity across contrasting environments. Thirty-five years of climate-driven simulations (1984–2018) showed strong spatiotemporal variability in stress exposure. Early sowing (October) predisposed crops to cold-induced spikelet sterility, whereas late sowing (mid-December onwards) intensified exposure to terminal salinity and heat stress, elevating irrigation demand while reducing water productivity. Mid-November sowing consistently minimized risk trade-offs, achieving the highest probabilities of exceeding 5.0 Mg ha−1 with superior irrigation water productivity (9–11 kg grain ha−1 mm−1). Salt-tolerant cultivars (e.g. BRRI Dhan67, WGL20471) maintained yield across variable stress environments, whereas susceptible genotypes (e.g. BRRI Dhan28, IET4786) exhibited high interannual yield variability and frequent failure. Sowing date and cultivar selection jointly determine Boro rice productivity and yield stability in coastal saline environments. Mid-November sowing, combined with salt-tolerant cultivars, emerged as a promising strategy for reducing climatic and salinity-related production risks. However, the magnitude of these benefits depends on local stress conditions and hydrological characteristics. The findings support a shift from blanket regional recommendations towards dynamic, simulation-based decision-support systems that integrate sowing windows, stress-resilient cultivars, and location-specific hydrological and salinity conditions. Integrating these systems into agricultural extension services and policy frameworks could improve climate resilience, irrigation water productivity, and sustainable Boro rice production across the coastal saline zones of South Asia.

title: Transient ATM inhibition enhances knock-in efficiency in hematopoietic stem cells by attenuating the DNA damage response.
abstract: Precise genome editing in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) holds great potential for treating inherited blood disorders; however, low knock-in (KI) efficiency and loss of functional HSCs after genome editing remain major obstacles. Here, we demonstrate that transient inhibition of Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated (ATM) kinase markedly enhanced KI efficiency in mouse HSCs genome-edited with Cas9/ribonucleoprotein (RNP) and AAV donor DNA. Phosphoproteomic and capillary western blot analyses revealed that ATM inhibition suppressed aberrant Cas9-AAV-induced ATM activation and the subsequent DNA damage response, reduced p53-dependent apoptosis, and enhanced survival of KI HSCs. In serial transplantation assays, ATM inhibition preserved long-term engrafting KI HSCs, increasing their frequency from ~0.3 to 40% in secondary recipients, an over 100-fold improvement. Furthermore, in an X-linked severe combined immunodeficient mouse model, ATM inhibition increased KI efficiency and restored T- and B cell differentiation. Comprehensive safety analyses, including long-read nanopore sequencing, amplicon deep sequencing, whole genome sequencing and clonal tracking, did not detect increased genomic alterations, chromosomal abnormalities, or clonal expansion following transient ATM inhibition. Taken together, these findings establish transient ATM inhibition as an effective strategy to enhance KI-mediated genome editing while maintaining the long-term repopulating capacity of HSCs.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: The impact of racist events on post-trauma mental health symptoms among immigrants and refugees in Canada: the role of racial trauma.
abstract: Background: Immigrants and refugees are at greater risk of mental health symptoms, including elevated symptoms of depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). For racialized immigrants and refugees, frequent exposure to racist events is one of several predictors of mental health outcomes. According to race-based traumatic stress theory, repeated exposure to racist events can undermine safety, belonging, and dignity, and may lead to racial trauma, referring to the psychological and physiological stress responses arising from such experiences. However, it remains unknown whether racial trauma plays a mediating role in the relationship between racist events and mental health symptoms. To address this gap, the present study aimed to examine racial trauma as a mediator of this relationship among racialized immigrants and refugees in Canada.Methods: A sample of 182 immigrants and refugees in Canada (Mage = 30.76; 52.2% men; 52.7% of African descent) completed self-report measures. The mediating role of racial trauma in the relationship between racist events and mental health symptoms (PTSD, depression, anxiety) was examined using PROCESS Model 4.Results: Results indicated that racial trauma significantly explained the relationship between racist events and mental health outcomes, including PTSD (B = 0.35, CI [0.20, 0.56]), depression (B = 0.11, CI [0.06, 0.18]), and anxiety (B = 0.12, CI [0.08, 0.17]). The model accounted for 34.02% to 46.21% of the variances in mental health outcomes.Conclusions: Among racialized immigrants and refugees, greater exposure to racist events was associated with elevated racial trauma, which contributed to higher PTSD, depression, and anxiety symptoms. Clinicians, community organizations, and policymakers should integrate anti-racism strategies and racial trauma frameworks to support the mental health of immigrants and refugees.

title: A Systematic Map of environmental and socio-economic effects in commercial bivalve production
abstract: Commercial bivalve systems underpin coastal economies, food provision, and livelihoods, yet evidence on how environmental exposures translate into socio-economic vulnerability remains fragmented. This systematic map aimed to characterise the peer-reviewed evidence base on the socio-economic outcomes of environmental exposures in commercial bivalve systems. Following Collaboration for Environmental Evidence guidelines and ROSES reporting standards, searches were conducted in Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, supported by citation chasing and organisational website searches. While initial screening sought out grey literature, only peer-reviewed articles met our empirical inclusion thresholds upon full-text review. Eligible studies were published in English from 2005 onwards and examined commercial bivalve systems, at least one environmental exposure, and at least one stakeholder-relevant socio-economic outcome. Included studies were coded for geography, bivalve type, system type, stakeholder group, exposure, outcome, and mitigation or adaptation response. Twenty-eight articles met the inclusion criteria. The evidence base was geographically concentrated, with the United States contributing the largest share of studies. Clams, mussels, and oysters were the most frequently represented bivalve groups. Temperature and ocean acidification were the dominant exposures, followed by storms, heatwaves, and pollution runoff. Revenue, cost, and yield or production were the most frequently reported socio-economic outcomes across stakeholder groups and exposure types, whereas labour, food security, health, and social outcomes were less commonly examined. Regulation, scenario planning, forecasting, and sustainable farming were the most frequently documented responses. Overall, the evidence base is strongest in documenting economic and production-related vulnerability to major climate stressors, but remains weaker on slower-onset exposures, broader wellbeing dimensions, underrepresented stakeholders, and diverse adaptation pathways.

title: Simulation of annual productivity and water dynamics of winter wheat-summer maize production system
abstract: This study focuses on the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping system and aims to develop an annual process model that can accurately simulate crop growth and development along with soil moisture dynamics. Based on the field split-plot experimental data that combined different varieties with sowing date treatments, a wheat-maize double-cropping production system model was built, incorporating modules for crop development stages, leaf area dynamics, biomass accumulation and partitioning, yield formation, and soil moisture balance. The model parameters were calibrated using 2008–2009 data, and validated with independent 2009–2010 data, and model performance in key physiological and ecological processes and in yield formation is systematically evaluated by using root mean square error (RMSE) and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Validation results show: 1) excellent simulation of crop phenology, with NRMSE for development stages at 1.87% for winter wheat and 5.36% for summer maize; 2) the model capture of leaf area index dynamics, with NRMSE of 27.52% for winter wheat and 11.96% for summer maize; 3) aboveground biomass accumulation was simulated with NRMSE of 16.02% for winter wheat and 15.50% for summer maize; 4) yield simulation achieved NRMSE of 5.78% for winter wheat and 17.80% for summer maize; 5) soil water storage in the 0–60 cm soil layer was simulated with good accuracy (NRMSE = 15.13%). Under the specific site conditions and the tested genotype-by-sowing-date combinations, the model demonstrated reasonable capability in simulating key processes of the winter wheat–summer maize production system.

title: Reproduction in Ferns: Gametophyte Development, Sex Determination, Gametogenesis, and Embryogenesis
abstract: Sexual reproduction in land plants has diversified over more than 500 million years of evolution. Ferns occupy a key phylogenetic position among land plants because they possess a dominant sporophyte, as in seed plants, while retaining a free-living gametophyte that produces gametes through mitotic divisions, as in bryophytes. This combination of life cycle features provides a useful framework for understanding how reproductive and developmental programs have evolved across land plants. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of fern reproduction, with particular emphasis on the model fern Ceratopteris richardii and the related species C. thalictroides. We focus on four interconnected processes: (1) gametophyte development and the meristem, which functions as a signaling center required for prothallus formation and gametangium positioning; (2) sex determination by antheridiogen, including classical genetic models, hormonal regulation, and recent studies linking meristem identity to sexual fate; (3) gametangium development and gametogenesis, covering antheridium and archegonium formation as well as the differentiation of motile sperm and egg cells; and (4) fertilization and embryogenesis, including gamete interaction, zygotic polarity, and embryonic axis formation. Recent advances in genome sequencing, transformation, genome editing, live imaging, and transcriptomic analyses are beginning to connect the rich morphological literature on ferns with molecular mechanisms. These advances make Ceratopteris a key comparative system for uncovering how reproductive structures, stem cell functions, and embryogenic programs have been conserved, modified, and redeployed during land plant evolution.

title: Post-Hoc Feature Selection Layer for Neural Networks Interpretability
abstract: The interpretability of complex neural networks remains a critical challenge, especially for models already deployed in high-stakes domains. To address this, we adapted the Feature Selection Layer (FSL) to optimize feature weights post-training, a variant we term post-hoc FSL. Our approach reframes the FSL as a lightweight, trainable module that integrates with already frozen pre-trained models on tabular datasets to highlight the features the original model considers most important. This post-hoc FSL learns feature relevance by fine-tuning its weights based on the original model's learned outputs. Crucially, this process is non-invasive, operating without altering the original model's architecture or its learned parameters. We conducted our experiments using both statistical and visual metrics, including accuracy, F1 score, recall, precision, weighted t-SNE and silhouette score, and also analyzed the stability of the post-hoc FSL on high-dimensional synthetic and real-world tabular datasets. We compared the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method using these metrics against the original embedded FSL and other post-hoc interpretability methods, such as Integrated Gradients, Noise Tunnel, DeepLIFT, Gradient SHAP, and Feature Ablation. Experimental results demonstrate that the post-hoc FSL feature weighting method successfully identified relevant features across the different datasets, maintaining the predictive power of the original neural network while enhancing its interpretability.

title: Data-Driven Vision-Language Models for Remote Sensing: A Survey
abstract: During the deep learning era, innovations in remote sensing (RS) vision models primarily focused on optimizing network architectures for specific tasks and conducting end-to-end training. However, with the advent of the Vision-Language Models (VLMs) era, constrained by substantial computational resource demands, the mainstream research paradigm has shifted towards adapting general-purpose VLMs using RS vertical domain data for fine-tuning, rather than modifying their core architectures. This transition marks a change in the innovation pathway from model-centric to data-centric. Despite the increasing importance of data, the academic community still lacks a systematic, data-centric survey to guide researchers in constructing high-quality RS vision-language datasets for various application scenarios and in conducting effective model fine-tuning and performance evaluation based on these datasets. To address this gap, this paper presents a systematic review of the development status of RS datasets tailored for VLMs. It further provides a comprehensive practical guide for RS researchers in the large model era, covering the entire pipeline from data construction to fine-tuning and evaluation. This paper aims to encourage the academic community to build more diverse and higher-quality vision-language datasets for specialized RS sub-fields. Ultimately, the goal is to converge these efforts into a comprehensive RS vision-language corpus that offers extensive task coverage and a wide geographical distribution, thereby laying a solid data foundation for advancing towards general artificial intelligence in RS.

title: Hydromorphological Restoration of Streams Does Not Ensure the Recovery of Ecosystem Functioning
abstract: Ecological restoration is widely expected to recover multiple ecosystem attributes, yet biological structure and ecosystem functioning may respond differently to hydromorphological restoration. Interpreting functional change is further complicated because higher or lower process rates do not inherently indicate recovery; their ecological meaning depends on how degraded and restored conditions compare with an appropriate reference state. We synthesised 582 effect sizes from 66 studies to quantify responses of nine ecosystem functions to hydromorphological restoration of streams and to assess whether changes in biological structure coincided with functional responses. Ecosystem‐function responses varied substantially among processes and baselines. Gross primary production was significantly higher in degraded than in reference streams, illustrating that elevated functional rates do not necessarily indicate reference‐like ecological conditions. Restoration did not consistently reverse degradation‐associated functional differences: denitrification was significantly lower in restored than in degraded streams, whereas nitrate uptake remained significantly lower in restored than in reference streams. Other restored–reference differences were generally weak or uncertain. Functional responses did not differ systematically among broad restoration‐measure categories. Restoration age was associated with changes in gross primary production and denitrification relative to degraded conditions, but none of the functions showed detectable convergence towards or divergence from reference conditions through time. In studies measuring both biological structure and ecosystem functioning, biological responses to restoration were generally positive relative to degraded conditions, whereas functional responses were more variable. However, the available evidence was too uncertain to conclude that biological and functional responses systematically differed. Our synthesis shows that functional recovery cannot be inferred either from restoration‐associated change alone or from concurrent biological recovery. Assessing restoration success therefore requires direct measurements of ecosystem processes and ecologically meaningful reference conditions that reveal whether functional change represents movement towards a process‐specific restoration target.

title: Non‐Linear Increases of Soil Carbon Stocks and Turnover Along Alpine Greening Gradients on Different Bedrocks
abstract: Alpine ecosystems are experiencing warming, leading to alpine greening—an upward migration and enhanced productivity of vegetation. Although soils represent the largest carbon (C) stocks in these ecosystems, impacts of greening on soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics remain unknown, especially in the high alpine zone. We measured SOC stocks, quality and radiocarbon ( 14 C) based turnover rates along elevation gradients from (sub)alpine forests to periglacial zones on three bedrock types, representing trajectories of changes in climate and vegetation and weathering regime. Data were linked to SOC stabilizing pedogenic oxides (PO) to assess the potential of soils to sequester C upon alpine greening. Results show pronounced decreases in SOC stocks (from 10 to 1 kg C m −2 ) and increases in 14 C‐based turnover times (from decades to millennia) with increasing elevation. This pattern followed a non‐linear sigmoidal function with a threshold at the vegetation line where grassland transitions to the nival zone. High alpine soils showed low SOC:PO ratios, indicating low C saturation and a high capacity to stabilize SOC on reactive minerals. However, negligible 14 C‐derived carbon inputs suggest that low vegetation productivity constrains SOC sequestration in these soils. In contrast, towards lower elevation with a warmer climate, grassland soils receive higher C inputs, but appear more C saturated, leading to greater SOC turnover but little SOC stock changes. Bedrock influenced SOC dynamics with approximately 50% smaller SOC stocks and faster turnover rates in dolomitic than in siliceous soils, due to slower weathering and lower SOC stabilization. Using elevation as a space‐for‐time substitution, we infer that SOC sequestration under alpine greening will be confined to areas around the vegetation line, with parent material influencing the magnitude of C uptake. Future projections of SOC dynamics should account for vegetation shifts and bedrock‐driven stabilization to constrain the role of alpine soils in land carbon‐climate feedbacks.

title: Qualitative development of the daily identity-related stress and resilience model using daily diaries from LGBTQ+ youth in the southeastern United States.
abstract: The prevailing reliance on cross-sectional methods in LGBTQ+ mental health research has limited researchers' ability to capture the dynamic, multilevel processes of minority stress and resilience factors as they unfold over time. Although socioecological frameworks have been applied longitudinally, they have rarely attended to the interplay of historical, developmental, and short-term timescales that shape LGBTQ+ youth's day-to-day experiences. Using qualitative daily diary data from a smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study, we pursued two aims: (1) to characterize LGBTQ+ youth's daily positive and negative identity-related experiences using qualitative content analysis; and (2) to develop a conceptual model illustrating how minority stress and resilience factors co-occur and unfold within daily life. Over 28 consecutive days, 50 LGBTQ+ youth aged 13-24 (Mage = 18.38, SD = 3.02; 58% transgender or gender-diverse) living in the U.S. Southeast and at elevated risk for suicide completed nightly diary entries describing the most positive and most negative event of their day. Qualitative content analysis of 349 identity-related diaries (108 negative, 241 positive) revealed that minority stress and resilience factors co-occurred across structural, interpersonal, and intrapersonal socioecological levels within single days, and that identity-related experiences showed meaningful continuity across days at the within-person level. Drawing on these findings and existing socioecological frameworks of minority stress, we developed the Daily Identity-Related Stress and Resilience Model, a conceptual framework that positions stress and resilience factors as simultaneous, multilevel processes embedded within individuals' daily lives and shaped by time-stable social and identity factors across both short- and long-term timescales. Implications for future research and intervention development with LGBTQ+ youth are discussed.

title: Molecular Basis of Silicon-Mediated Plant Defense: Transporters, Cell Wall Integrity, Redox-Hormone Crosstalk, and Epigenetic Priming.
abstract: Silicon (Si) is emerging as a key modulator, and its molecular mechanism of defense regulation keeps emerging. This review focus on Si-uptake by Lsi-type transporters, deposition in cuticles and cell wall, redox buffering, modify cell wall integrity (CWI) and hormonal signaling to increase resistance against adverse conditions and to reshape plant-microbe-soil interaction in rhizosphere. By highlighting the emerging research on Si-mediated regulations at molecular scale, we proposed two working hypotheses which are 'mechanical buffer model' for soluble-Si and 'dynamic signaling model' for Si-nanomaterials (Si-NPs). Mechanical buffer model states that Si-fortified walls could stabilize the ROS profile and wall mechanics to maintain and primed state for cell while dynamic signaling model states that Si-NPs follow an additional vesicle-mediated uptake forming a corona protein, elicit ROS-bursts, robust activation of FERONIA-like receptors, Ca2+ channels, and JA/SA signaling. Furthermore, association of Si-associated chromatin and siRNAs were summarized and how these Si-mediated alterations in DNA methylation under stress conditions could support the stress memory and defense priming. Overall, this framework could provide a molecular basis for Si-mediated inputs and breeding approaches with the aim of climate-resilient crops.

title: Calculation of grid boundary scale for global submarine topography model
abstract: To address the issue that current submarine terrain grid scales do not adequately consider the influences of water depth, bathymetric instrument performance, and other factors, this paper proposes a grid boundary scale calculation method for global submarine topography models that takes into account multi-beam beam angles. First, original data grids are constructed based on global submarine topography models, cropped and segmented to establish small image datasets for extraction and screening algorithms. Second, attribute values of small images are extracted in batches through parallel algorithms, and data are extracted and screened to establish attribute datasets for submarine terrain grid scale parameter calculations. Third, the lateral scale of local submarine terrain grids is calculated with the multi-beam beam angle as the primary factor, while the longitudinal scale is calculated with navigation speed and sampling period as the primary factors; the local submarine terrain complexity is used as a weight to process the grid scale, thereby constructing a submarine terrain grid scale calculation model under the combined influence of multiple factors including beam angle, navigation speed, sampling period, and terrain complexity. Finally, this model is applied to dynamic solutions across global ocean areas to generate raster images of grid boundary scales for global submarine topography models. Experimental results show that this method can identify submarine topographic forms and calculate the theoretical minimum grid scale within regions while considering multi-beam beam angles, providing theoretical support for constructing variable-resolution submarine terrain grid models.

title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
abstract: The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. In this work, we report on a sizable thermal Hall conductivity in nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS 3 ), a van der Waals stack of honeycomb layers with a zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The longitudinal (κ aa ) and the transverse (κ ab ) thermal conductivities peak at the same temperature, and the thermal Hall angle, at this peak, respects a previously identified bound. The amplitude of κ ab is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the b axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.

title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd 5 AlI 2 , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd 5 AlI 2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity
abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death
abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. Activation of BAX-BAK without apoptosome activation triggers sustained efflux of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and caspase-independent cell death. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation–induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer
abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti–programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels
abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.

title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals
abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter’s states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra–unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.

title: Decoupled self-assembled monolayer and perovskite deposition for efficient flexible solar modules
abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization. The certified PCE with phenethylammonium iodide as the passivation molecule was 20.2% on PSMs with device areas of 750 cm 2 . With 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide as the passivator, the PCE of 22.0% for a device area of 14.55 cm 2 decreased by 8% after 1044 hours under maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices pass all sequences of an international commercialization assessment standard for flexible portable PSMs.

title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria
abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

title: Generalized continuous nowhere differentiable function families
abstract: The existence of continuous nowhere-differentiable functions is a fundamental phenomenon in real analysis, challenging the classical intuition that continuity generally implies differentiability. Once regarded as pathological constructions, such functions are now recognized as abundant in the space of continuous functions, both in the sense of Baire category and through notions of prevalence. In this paper, we develop a general framework for constructing continuous nowhere differentiable functions represented by trigonometric series with decaying amplitudes and rapidly increasing frequencies. We establish a sufficient condition for nowhere differentiability that applies to a broad class of Fourier-type series, thereby providing a unified criterion that encompasses several classical constructions, including the Weierstrass function and related examples. The proposed approach also yields new families of continuous nowhere differentiable functions under flexible conditions on the amplitudes and frequencies. These results contribute to a systematic understanding of the mechanisms underlying the breakdown of differentiability and further illustrate the richness and ubiquity of nowhere-differentiable behavior within the class of continuous functions.

title: Exploring the Dark Tetrad in Human–GenAI Relationships: A Multi-Source Evaluation of GenAI Abuse
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) companions become increasingly integrated into users’ social lives, concerns have arisen regarding the potential for abuse of these artificial agents. Some scholars have further suggested that such abusive behaviors toward GenAI may eventually spill over into human interpersonal contexts. Guided by the Realistic Accuracy Model (RAM), this study investigated how Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy, and sadism predict emotionally abusive behavior toward GenAI companions. A dyadic design was employed, collecting parallel reports from both human users (self-reports) and their GenAI companions (GenAI assessments) among 1041 participants (632 females; average age = 25.10 years) recruited from an online human–GenAI relationship community. Results demonstrated that psychopathy and sadism were consistent predictors of GenAI abuse across both reporting perspectives, whereas narcissism exhibited a stable negative association with abuse. In contrast, Machiavellianism predicted GenAI abuse only through GenAI assessments, but not self-reports. Theoretically, our findings extend RAM to human–AI relationships, demonstrating that personality traits vary in how accurately they can be judged in GenAI contexts. Practically, the results highlight that individuals high in certain Dark Tetrad traits—specifically psychopathy and sadism—represent personality-driven high-risk groups, providing insights for practitioners in education and technology to develop interventions or safeguards aimed at mitigating abusive behavior toward GenAI companions.

title: Factors Associated with Adverse Effects of Postoperative TSH-Directed Levothyroxine Therapy in Adults with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: A Scoping Review.
abstract: BACKGROUND Postoperative thyrotropin (TSH)-directed levothyroxine is used to reduce recurrence risk in selected patients with differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), but treatment-related adverse effects may vary based on patient susceptibility and treatment exposure. Contemporary guidelines increasingly require balancing anticipated oncologic benefit against potential harm. This scoping review synthesizes patient-, treatment-, and disease-related factors associated with adverse effects of postoperative TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy in adults with DTC. METHODS This scoping review was reported following PRISMA-ScR guidelines and prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework. MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from January 1, 2011, to February 24, 2026. Eligible studies reported associations between patient-, treatment-, or disease-related factors and adverse effects among adults with DTC receiving postoperative TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy. Data were summarized descriptively and synthesized narratively, with stratification according to TSH exposure definition. RESULTS Of 7361 records screened, 35 studies including 11,819 patients were included. Skeletal outcomes were most frequently reported (51.4%), followed by cardiometabolic (40.0%), neuropsychological (11.4%), reproductive (2.9%), and muscular outcomes (2.9%). TSH exposure definitions varied substantially: 18 studies evaluated subnormal TSH, 2 low-normal TSH, 8 mixed categories spanning subnormal and low-normal TSH, 4 continuous biochemical/treatment measures, and 3 unclear exposures. Greater suppression intensity was the most consistently reported treatment-related factor associated with adverse skeletal outcomes, particularly in studies evaluating subnormal TSH. Longer treatment duration was associated with skeletal harm in selected studies. Postmenopausal status emerged as a relatively consistent patient-level factor, whereas associations with age and body mass index were variable. Evidence for cardiometabolic, neuropsychological, reproductive, and muscular outcomes was less extensive and less consistent, and disease-related factors were infrequently examined. Only two studies conducted prediction/discrimination analyses, both involving skeletal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS Evidence on adverse effects associated with TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy in DTC is most consistent for skeletal outcomes and predominantly derives from studies evaluating subnormal TSH exposure. The available literature provides limited evidence for clinically applicable prediction of toxicity or cumulative treatment burden. Future longitudinal studies should better characterize the intensity and persistence of biochemical exposure and develop outcome-specific prediction models integrating baseline susceptibility, organ vulnerability, and longitudinal treatment exposure to support individualized TSH management.
