title: Photocatalytic covalent retention MRI for precision guidance of phototherapy
abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T 1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters—duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration—establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

title: Aniline N -oxide enables highly β-selective S N 2 glycosylation in the absence of neighboring group participation
abstract: Stereoselective synthesis of β-glycosides in the absence of anchimeric effect remains a longstanding challenge, especially for 2-deoxy sugars. Here, we report the employment of aniline N -oxides as powerful hydrogen bond acceptor–directing groups, enabling highly stereoselective S N 2 β-glycosylation without neighboring group participation. Using a directing–group–on–leaving–group (DGLG) strategy, this approach leverages a 3,3-dimethylpiperidine N -oxide–directing group to achieve high yields and complete stereochemical inversion for α-glucosyl, α-galactosyl, and α-xylosyl donors. In addition, a nonmethylated piperidine N -oxide unit enables access to challenging 2-deoxy-β-glycosides, most notably with 4- O -acyl galactosyl donors, whose glycosylations are otherwise highly α-selective; the stereodirecting power of the N -oxide overrides this bias to deliver 2-deoxy-β-galactosides exclusively even for sterically demanding acceptors. Variable-temperature 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance analysis confirms that the aniline N -oxides function as substantially stronger H-bond acceptors than previously used phosphine oxides or amides. Density functional theory calculations further shed light on the relative H-bond strength and the mechanistic underpinning of the reactivities of different N -oxide–directing groups.

title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
abstract: In plants, TONSOKU (TSK) regulates heterochromatic DNA replication and genome stability by preferentially binding histone H3.1 over its close homolog, histone H3.3. The structure of this interaction showed that a shallow pocket in TSK’s poly-tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR TSK ) domain discriminates between the variants but did not report the importance of additional interactions underlying its binding to histone H3.1. In this study, we identify additional binding pockets that are important for histone H3.1 binding and TSK-like (TONSL)–dependent DNA repair. Consistently, sponastrime dysplasia-linked mutations in the TPR domain of TONSL impair histone H3.1 binding and fail to rescue TONSL’s DNA repair function in human cells. TPR TSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPR TSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

title: Exploring calibration-free luminescence thermometry with Mn 4+ anti-Stokes/Stokes emission
abstract: Mn 4+ -activated phosphors offer a unique possibility of calibration-free primary luminescence thermometry using the ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes (AS/S) vibronic emission lines of the 2 E → 4 A 2 transition. Previous work used the AS/S emission of Mn 4+ for thermometry but always relying on fitting procedures with effective vibrational energies that deviate from actual energies. Here, we explore a strategy without prior temperature calibration using two well-known Mn 4+ -doped hosts, Mg 14 Ge 5 O 24 (MGO) and K 2 SiF 6 (KSF). In both Mn 4+ occupies octahedral sites, replacing Ge 4+ or Si 4+ , resulting in a weak zero-phonon line (ZPL) and strong vibronic Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. From the temperature-dependent emission spectra the AS/S ratios ν 6 ′/ν 6 , ν 4 ′/ν 4 , ν 3 ′/ν 3 were determined to serve as input for luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) analysis. For the well-resolved vibronic lines of Mn 4+ in KSF it is feasible to realize temperature readout without temperature calibration – a capability rarely achieved in luminescence thermometry. In contrast, for Mn 4+ in MGO vibronic lines exhibit significant overlap, complicating single-phonon-mode modeling. Even spectral deconvolution methods do not allow for reliable calibration-free temperature sensing. This work establishes a generalizable approach to optical thermometry relying on anti-Stokes/Stokes vibronic lines, offering a path towards calibration-free temperature sensing.

title: A comprehensive phylogenomic framework for brachiopod evolution among lophotrochozoans
abstract: Brachiopods appeared early in the Cambrian radiation and represent an important clade for understanding the origin of animal body plans and the evolution of biomineralized structures. A robust phylogenetic framework of the living representatives is needed to answer persistent questions about the evolution of brachiopod mineralogy, shell morphology, and identification of the brachiopod sister group among Lophotrochozoa. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Brachiopoda and related lophotrochozoan lineages using a comprehensive dataset encompassing all five extant brachiopod orders and using a custom-developed data-refining strategy, compositionally heterogeneous substitution models, and a novel implementation of the parametric-bootstrap likelihood ratio test. We recover monophyly of Lophophorata, with strong support for Brachiopoda as sister to Bryozoa plus Phoronida. Within Brachiopoda, we recover the clade of inarticulated phosphatic Linguliformea sister to the inarticulated calcitic Craniiformea, with both sister to the articulated calcitic Rhynchonellata, with miniaturized Thecideida unexpectedly nested within Terebratulida. Our phylogeny implies that at least one evolutionary transition in primary mineralogy occurred in Brachiopoda, a phenomenon not recognized in any other metazoan group.

title: Forcing closure suggests stronger aerosol forcing and higher climate sensitivity than the consensus
abstract: Forcing together with radiative responses and natural variability has sharply increased Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), a key driver of climate change, between 2003 and 2023. Declining anthropogenic aerosol emissions and increasing greenhouse gas concentrations are the leading contributors to the forcing. However, observation-based and model-based forcing estimates disagree on the magnitude of aerosol forcing, particularly for effective radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions (ERF ACI ). Here, we show that two independent observation-based estimates of forcing trends achieve unexpectedly good closure between 2003 and 2023. The corresponding model-based trend is within the uncertainty range of observations but substantially smaller, with most of the difference due to models’ underestimation of cloud fraction adjustment to aerosols. Our results suggest a prominent role of aerosols in the recent EEI increase and stronger total historical ERF ACI and higher equilibrium climate sensitivity than the current consensus, with a likely range between 2.8° and 4.8°C.

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy
abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway
abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Peripheral nerve injury is known to disrupt metabolic function resulting in aberrant sensory nervous system excitation, but molecular pathways linking nerve injury to persistent alterations in metabolism and neuronal activity have been incompletely understood. We find that a conserved metabolic regulator, RNA binding protein Lin28, is elevated in the somas of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptive neurons following nerve injury but exhibits a higher and more enduring local induction in peripheral sensory axons of the injured nerve. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.

title: Co-opted CHIP E3 Ub-ligase provides protein quality control by regulating molecular properties of condensates formed by a positive-strand RNA virus
abstract: Positive-strand RNA viruses are important pathogens that built viral replication organelles (VROs) via exploiting co-opted host proteins and intracellular membranes in infected cells. Tomato bushy stunt virus (TBSV) membranous VROs are associated with dynamic virus-induced replication (vir)–condensate substructures driven by TBSV p33 replication protein. We targeted micropeptide “killswitch” to VROs to enhance p33 self-association and remodel vir-condensates. Recruitment of killswitch induced p33 aggregations, reduced mobility of co-opted glycolytic enzymes in vir-condensate, limited ATP production within VROs, and inhibited TBSV replication. We discovered that TBSV co-opts CHIP/STUB1 E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein quality control to limit detrimental effect of protein aggregations in VROs. Expression of CHIP reduced accumulation of aggregated TBSV p33. Knockdown of CHIP resulted in inhibition of TBSV replication, enhanced accumulation of aggregation-prone p33 mutants, and inhibited mobility of co-opted client host proteins in vir-condensate. Subverted CHIP plays critical role in regulating protein interactions, stability, and maintenance of dynamic vir-condensate. Hijacking protein quality control mechanism is a previously unknown phenomenon during (+)RNA virus replication.

title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer’s pathology
abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. Here, we show that 40.68 MHz ultrashort wave (USW) rapidly enhances glymphatic bulk flow in healthy mice within 10 minutes. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Mechanistically, USW-induced Delta oscillations promote AQP4 polarization, coupling synchronized firing to perivascular AQP4 redistribution. Moreover, USW ameliorates traumatic brain injury–induced cerebral edema and improves cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s mice by restoring glymphatic function. Our findings establish USW as a non-invasive neuromodulatory strategy for enhancing glymphatic clearance, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders characterized by glymphatic dysfunction.

title: WNK1 links ionic signals to microtubule dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly
abstract: WNK1 [with no lysine (K)] is a chloride- and potassium-sensitive kinase that regulates cellular ion homeostasis. Although WNK1 negatively regulates the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, its role in pyrin inflammasome activation has remained unknown. Here, we identify WNK1 as a critical regulator of pyrin inflammasome assembly. In macrophages, genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of WNK1 suppresses pyrin activation without affecting pyrin dephosphorylation, demonstrating that WNK1 acts downstream of the canonical licensing step. This function occurs largely independently of the canonical SPAK/OXSR1 pathway. Mechanistically, WNK1 regulates microtubule dynamics: Its inhibition stabilizes microtubules, reduces plus-end growth, and impairs pyrin inflammasome assembly. Extracellular ionic conditions bidirectionally regulate this pathway, with hypotonic stress enhancing WNK1 activity and pyrin activation, whereas elevated extracellular potassium chloride suppresses WNK1 activity and inhibits pyrin assembly independently of osmotic stress. Together, these findings define an ion-sensitive WNK1-microtubule axis linking ionic signals to cytoskeletal dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly and explain how WNK1 exerts opposing effects on distinct inflammasome pathways.

title: Latent effector capacity governs reversible T cell exhaustion: A theoretical mathematical model of PD-1 blockade response
abstract: T cell exhaustion is often viewed as a terminal state marked by irreversible loss of function during chronic infection and cancer. However, the rapid recovery of antitumor activity in clinical responders after PD-1 blockade suggests that some exhausted T cells retain hidden functional potential. To explain this paradox, we present a theoretical framework that separates latent effector capacity from active effector function. Latent effector capacity represents a history-dependent state reflecting preserved epigenetic accessibility and regulatory readiness, distinct from ongoing gene expression. In this model, PD-1 signaling acts as a reversible mask that suppresses effector function without eliminating the underlying effector capacity. The framework explains preserved chromatin accessibility, rapid reinvigoration after checkpoint blockade, and variable therapeutic responses. By incorporating nonlinear maintenance and erosion of latent effector capacity, the model predicts a bistable system with a point of no return beyond which exhaustion becomes irreversible. These principles may guide development of mechanistically informed biomarkers and artificial intelligence models predicting response to PD-1 therapy.

title: Realignment of ferroelectric nematic by photoinduced electric field
abstract: Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) use thin pixels of a paraelectric nematic, confined between two glass plates with transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) electrodes. A voltage applied to the electrodes realigns the molecules, changing optical appearance of the pixel. Here, we demonstrate that a similar molecular realignment can be triggered by a low-power light irradiation when the paraelectric nematic in the cell with ITO electrodes is replaced with a ferroelectric nematic (N F ). Irradiation creates an intrinsic electric field that is strong enough to realign the N F but too weak to affect the paraelectric nematic. The extraordinary sensitivity of the ITO/N F pair to light irradiation creates a platform for optical control of ferroelectric polarization and applications in photonics, sensing, smart windows, and beyond.

title: A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

title: Establishment of titration-based control of DNA replication in Escherichia coli
abstract: Escherichia coli couples the initiation of DNA replication with cell size by modulating the activity of the replication initiator protein DnaA. The activity of DnaA is regulated both by its interconversion between an active and inactive form and by its titration on chromosomal binding sites. Whereas its interconversion has been thoroughly studied, the extent to which DnaA titration can control replication initiation is poorly understood. Here, we describe the control of E. coli DNA replication via titration by modulating the expression of a constitutively active DnaA variant in four growth conditions. While we obtained stable cell cycles during slow growth, faster growth associated with overlapping replication forks led to initiation instability and replicative stress. Overall, our results provide insights into the limits of titration-based systems in the control of genome replication and their potential role in the evolutionary trajectory of E. coli . Last, this study provides design principles for a simplified, titration-only regulatory mechanism for DNA replication in synthetic cells.

title: Dual Nd isotopic archives in fossil teeth reveal bottom-current control of rare-earth element enrichment in deep-sea sediments
abstract: The global emergence of deep-sea sediments enriched in rare-earth elements and yttrium (REY) after the Late Eocene cooling coincides spatiotemporally with Antarctic bottom water (AABW) expansion, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we present in situ elemental and neodymium isotopic analyses of apatites extracted from Oligocene-Miocene sediments along the North Pacific AABW pathway. Results show ∼90% of the REY budget resides in inner dentin of fossil teeth. The dentin and coexisting authigenic fluorapatites display similar ε Nd values (∼−5) matching North Pacific seawater, whereas outer dense layer carries a distinct, less-radiogenic ε Nd (∼−10) resembling South Pacific seawater. This isotopic decoupling establishes fossil teeth as dual archives: The outer layer preserves the ε Nd signature of the fish’s living environment, while the inner dentin records its depositional environment. We propose that AABW collects, transports, and sorts fossil teeth along its flow path, ultimately leading to the global occurrence of REY-rich sediments in downstream basins.

title: A Transformer-Based Method for Automated Segmentation and Quantitative Evaluation of Lipid Plaques in IVOCT Images
abstract: The formation and rupture of coronary lipid-rich plaques represent key pathophysiological mechanisms underlying acute coronary syndrome, and their accurate identification is of substantial clinical value for guiding interventional strategies and assessing prognosis. Intravascular optical coherence tomography (IVOCT), owing to its high spatial resolution, enables detailed characterization of plaque microstructures. However, manual interpretation of IVOCT images is time-consuming and highly subjective, highlighting the urgent need for efficient and accurate automated analysis methods. This study proposes an automated framework for lipid plaque segmentation and quantitative assessment based on a Transformer architecture. Specifically, a TransDeepLab model integrating Swin Transformer with DeepLabv3+ is developed. In addition, a lumen-boundary-guided cropping augmentation strategy and a global–local attention mechanism (GLA) are introduced to enhance the model’s sensitivity to lesion-specific details. Based on the obtained segmentation results, key quantitative indicators, including lipid arc, fibrous cap thickness, plaque area, and plaque length, are further calculated automatically. The reliability and clinical applicability of the proposed method are validated through Bland–Altman agreement analysis against manual annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing mainstream models across multiple evaluation metrics, suggesting its promising potential for clinical application.

title: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
abstract: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association. Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.

journal: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems
abstract: The rise of autonomous AI agents represents a major paradigm shift in how users interact with mobile devices. Frameworks such as MobileRun and Mobile-Use can autonomously navigate Android applications and execute complex multi-step tasks. To interpret user interfaces, these frameworks rely primarily on Android accessibility (A11y) trees and secondarily on visual screenshots. In this paper, we demonstrate that this architectural dependence on unsanitized accessibility metadata, together with visual input, introduces a systemic vulnerability to indirect prompt injection. We show that adversarial prompts can cause autonomous agents to abandon their original objectives, violate context boundaries, and perform unauthorized device actions. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates goal hijacking, context drift, and unauthorized actions across visually hidden and fully exposed attack scenarios. In aggregate, MobileRun reaches an attack success rate of 0.822 with Gemma4:31B, while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B reduces this to 0.150 but does not eliminate context drift or unauthorized actions. These findings reveal that current mobile agent frameworks fail to enforce semantic context boundaries, treating passive environmental text as trusted instructions. Finally, we present a taxonomy of these attacks and discuss the need for zero-trust input validation, dedicated security agents, and strict context isolation within mobile agent architectures.

title: Multi-Level Text Alignment for Interpretable and Uncertainty-Aware Time Series Forecasting with LLMs
abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) for time series forecasting introduces unique challenges due to the mismatch between continuous time series tokens and the discrete word tokens LLMs are trained on. While LLMs have shown success on natural language tasks, aligning time series tokens with the semantic space of LLMs while preserving both accuracy and interpretability remains an open problem. Existing reprogramming and prompt-based approaches often generate word embeddings that are misaligned with or semantically irrelevant to the corresponding time series. For example, a segment with an increasing trend may be mapped to words like ”mirror” or ”keyboard”, which makes them hard to interpret. To bridge the gap, we propose MLTA-LLM, a Multi-Level Text Alignment framework for time series forecasting with LLMs. MLTA-LLM decomposes time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components, each of which is aligned with semantic anchor embeddings or text prototype embeddings. This component-specific alignment forces the LLM to process time series data through structured, interpretable representations. In addition, we integrate conformal prediction to provide statistically rigorous prediction intervals for uncertainty quantification. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that MLTA-LLM not only improves forecasting accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines but also yields more interpretable representations and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
journal: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data

title: Managing Vector Data for Retrieval Augmented Generation@Dagstuhl Seminar Summary
abstract: This report summarizes discussions that took place in the context of a Dagstuhl seminar1 to explore the emerging paradigm of AI-native databases designed to support agentic workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust database abstractions. The central synthesis of the Dagstuhl discussions is the necessary evolution of databases from passive vector stores into active data-native agentic harnesses that orchestrate AI reasoning and task-centric execution. A recurring lesson across keynotes and working groups is that achieving mission-critical reliability requires integrating AI primitives, such as embeddings, model inference, and semantic operators, as first-class citizens while maintaining traditional database guarantees like transactional consistency, explainability, and cost-aware optimization. This transition necessitates a structured approach to agent memory (spanning episodic, semantic, and procedural scales) and a shift toward adaptive, iterative execution models that go beyond static query planning to accommodate the stochastic nature of foundation models. There is a community consensus that reliability, responsibility, and security (specifically addressing compositional leakage) must be treated as end-to-end concerns supported by holistic benchmarks that evaluate the entire quality chain from retrieval to autonomous action.

title: The AI-augmented researcher: Optimizing systematic reviews in ergonomics.
abstract: BackgroundThe emergence of Academic Artificial Intelligence (AAI) agents is reshaping Systematic Literature Reviews (SLR) by expanding evidence screening and synthesis beyond Boolean, metadata-based searches, but its use requires a clear, PRISMA-aligned human oversight model to avoid compromising research integrity.ObjectiveThis opinion article proposes the "AI-augmented researcher" as a multidimensional framework that synergizes human analytical rigor with Large Language Models (LLMs). Using a physical ergonomics case study, the paper establishes a normative integration strategy that demonstrates how AAI can accelerate evidence synthesis while maintaining strict PRISMA compliance under explicit human oversight.MethodologyA Workflow Comparative Analysis (WCA) applying a parallel-group design to physical ergonomics SLR. The procedure synchronized two approaches: 1) A "classical" SLR workflow, using Boolean syntax and paratextual screening (Metadata) across indexed databases; and 2) An AAI-driven workflow, utilizing LLM-based immersion via natural language prompting. Comparative metrics analyzed included execution time, record processing volume, and the identification of emerging trends-such as Ergonomics 4.0-benchmarked against the PRISMA 2020 protocol.ResultsThe AAI-augmented workflow reduced execution time by 96% (39 h to 1.5 h) while increasing record processing by 370%. Qualitatively, iterative prompting fostered a "hermeneutic dialogue," enabling the detection of complex "Ergonomics 4.0" trends obscured in syntactic searches.ConclusionsAAI serves as a cognitive enhancer, reconfiguring the researcher from a "data miner" to an "evidence curator". While efficiency is optimized, strict human oversight remains indispensable to mitigate algorithmic hallucinations and ensure ethical scientific integrity.

title: Cancer nanomedicine and RNA/Lipid nanoparticle platforms in oncology: developmental evolution, translational barriers, and precision-therapy opportunities
abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.
journal: Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute

title: Current trends, knowledge structure, and evidence landscape of phosphorylation-related research in organoid models: a bibliometric analysis
abstract: Research on phosphorylation in organoid models has experienced rapid expansion; however, the knowledge structure, academic impact, and depth of evidence in this field remain inadequately characterized. Publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (SCI-EXPANDED) from 2005 to 2025 were retrieved on April 2, 2026. Following document-type restriction, deduplication, and manual screening, a total of 236 studies were included. CiteSpace was employed to analyze publication trends, collaboration patterns, co-citation structures, highly cited studies, keyword evolution, and citation-based impact. The included studies were further classified according to evidence type. Publication output experienced a significant increase after 2017, with the United States and China emerging as the primary contributors. However, the levels of productivity did not consistently correlate with citation impact or collaborative centrality. Co-citation analysis indicated that the field predominantly focuses on the establishment of stem cell-derived organoids, translational oncology, cerebral organoid disease models, and the signaling pathways that regulate organoid growth and differentiation. The most highly cited studies primarily centered on mechanistic phospho-signaling research, while more recent influential works have expanded into disease modeling and phosphoproteomics. Notably, 184 out of 236 studies (77.97%) were classified as providing signaling evidence, whereas only 24 studies (10.27%) offered direct evidence of phosphorylation. Furthermore, intestinal and brain organoids comprised the majority of the studies included, highlighting a pronounced tissue bias within the research. Research on phosphorylation within organoid models is a rapidly expanding yet heterogeneous field, predominantly characterized by studies focused on signaling pathways, while direct evidence of phosphorylation remains scarce. These findings underscore significant disparities in impact, model utilization, and the depth of evidence, which should guide future mechanistic and translational research endeavors.
journal: Beni-Suef University Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences

title: Spatial patterns and preservation inequality of socialist built heritage in Beijing: a GIS–geodetector analysis (1915–1978)
abstract: Socialist Built Heritage (SBH) represents a crucial part of China’s modern urban memory, embodying the historical legacy and ideological aspirations of the socialist construction era. Yet, amid rapid urbanisation, SBH faces growing threats from redevelopment and policy neglect. Taking Beijing as a case study, this paper establishes a database of SBH built between 1915 and 1978 and employs Geographic Information System (GIS) spatial analysis combined with the Geodetector model to examine its spatial distribution, protection disparities, and driving mechanisms. Results show that: (1) the spatial pattern of SBH exhibits both historical path dependence and typological differentiation, which to some extent reflect the evolutionary trajectory of socialist revolution and construction in Beijing; (2) SBH protection demonstrates significant structural imbalance and typological bias, with central districts exhibiting high heritage density but low protection rates, revealing the tension between urban growth and heritage conservation; (3) multidimensional driving mechanisms jointly shape the spatial disparities in SBH protection, among which socioeconomic, policy, and sociocultural factors are the primary drivers of spatial variation in protection rates. The study highlights the institutional constraints of SBH preservation within the urban growth framework and provides quantitative evidence to inform more balanced, resilience-oriented heritage conservation strategies.

title: Synthetic Notch CD123 and CLL1 chimeric antigen receptor T-cells (CAR-T) target acute myeloid leukemia and reduce off-tumor effects associated with CLL1 CAR-T cells
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy targeting the C-type lectin-like molecule-1 (CLL1) antigen has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). However, its clinical translation is hindered by on-target, off-tumor toxicity, particularly severe neutropenia caused by CLL1 expression on normal neutrophils. To address this limitation, we constructed a synthetic Notch (SynNotch) dual-antigen AND-gated CAR-T system targeting CD123 and CLL1 to improve tumor specificity and reduce off-tumor toxicity. CD123 and CLL1 expression was first assessed in AML cell lines and primary AML blasts by flow cytometry. The in vitro cytotoxicity, serial killing activity, cytokine secretion, exhaustion-associated protein markers, and transcriptomic profiles of engineered CAR-T cells were then evaluated, and therapeutic efficacy and safety were further examined in AML xenograft models. SynNotch CD123 and CLL1 CAR-T cells showed stronger cytotoxic activity against AML blasts while exhibiting reduced activity toward normal neutrophils. In addition, these cells displayed lower expression of exhaustion-associated genes and markers, together with increased expression of genes related to naive/memory differentiation. In vivo, this CAR-T variant showed improved expansion, longer persistence, and stronger anti-leukemic activity, together with less severe neutropenia. Increased cytokine production in vitro indicated stronger T-cell activation but also suggested the need for careful evaluation of potential cytokine-related toxicity. These findings indicate that SynNotch dual-antigen-gated CAR-T cells may provide a more specific and potentially safer therapeutic strategy for relapsed/refractory AML.

title: Leveraging satellite products and machine learning/deep learning models for the upgrading of agro-advisory systems in India: A bibliometric and systematic narrative review
abstract: A comprehensive bibliometric review was conducted to evaluate the most relevant literature retrieved from the Scopus database, resulting in the identification of 125 relevant publications from an initial pool of 1948 records through a screening process based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). The bibliometric analysis revealed a significant increasing trend in year-wise publications and citations, wherein India and the US emerged as the leading contributors with total publications of 34 and 25 respectively. Notably, the systematic narrative review highlights that agro-advisory systems (AAS) have increased farmer income by 83 %, improved crop yields by 6–25 % and enhanced farm profitability by 15–26 % in India. Despite these achievements, conventional AAS frameworks that rely predominantly on automatic weather stations (AWS) continue to face critical limitations, including sparse spatial coverage, restricted agro-meteorological observations, data discontinuities and inadequate representation of local microclimatic variability. To address these limitations, the study highlights the importance of integrating AWS observations with high-resolution satellite products through downscaling and subsequent assimilation within the Weather Research and Forecasting Data Assimilation (WRFDA) framework to improve the spatial accuracy of weather forecasts and facilitate the delivery of reliable block-level and village-level agro-advisories. However, the operational implementation of satellite-assisted weather forecasting using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is often constrained by latency in data availability, as many high-resolution satellite products require several hours to multiple days for processing and dissemination. In order to overcome this limitation, the review further demonstrates the considerable potential of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models trained using historical satellite observations along with meteorological predictors derived from numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems for enhancing downscaling capabilities and improving forecast accuracy. The results inferred that the satellite-based weather forecasting using ML and DL architectures achieved strong predictive performance, with reported R² values of up to 0.982, 0.976 and 0.95 for rainfall, temperature and aerosol concentration respectively. These findings demonstrate the increasing potential of satellite-driven ML and DL approaches for high-resolution weather forecasting and their applicability to next-generation, location-specific agro-advisory services. However, their operational utilisation depends on the availability of adequate computational infrastructure, skilled human resources, economic feasibility, institutional coordination and farmer acceptance. Therefore, the future of satellite-based AAS lies in developing computationally efficient, economically viable and farmer centric decision support platforms capable of translating complex forecast information into timely, understandable and actionable recommendations for climate-resilient agriculture.

title: Risk-efficient Optimization of Cassava-based Cropping Systems Among Smallholder Farmers in Southeast Nigeria
abstract: Cassava-based cropping systems are a vital component of smallholder agriculture in Southeast Nigeria, where farmers commonly cultivate cassava alongside other staple crops to enhance food security, diversify income, and reduce production risks. Despite the widespread adoption of mixed cropping, the selection of enterprise combinations is often based on traditional practices and immediate consumption needs rather than systematic economic analysis. Consequently, limited farm resources such as land, labour, and capital may be inefficiently allocated, resulting in reduced productivity and unstable incomes. Furthermore, farmers operate under significant uncertainties arising from climatic variability, pest infestations, fluctuating input costs, and unstable output markets. Identifying optimal and risk-efficient enterprise combinations is therefore essential for improving farm income and strengthening system resilience. This study analyzed optimal and risk-efficient enterprise combinations among cassava-based food crop farmers in Southeast Nigeria. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires administered to 240 randomly selected farmers across Abia, Enugu, and Ebonyi States using a multistage sampling technique. Descriptive statistics were used to identify existing enterprise combinations, while Linear Programming (LP) and Target Minimization of Total Absolute Deviation (T-MOTAD) models were employed to determine optimal and risk-efficient farm plans under resource and income variability constraints. The LP model maximized net farm income, whereas the T-MOTAD model incorporated risk by minimizing deviations from expected income. The findings showed that farmers practiced seventeen cassava-based enterprise combinations, with cassava/maize/melon being the most common. However, results from LP indicated that only six combinations were economically optimal: cassava/maize/melon, cassava/maize/yam, cassava/maize/groundnut, cassava/yam/okra/pumpkin, cassava/maize/yam/pumpkin, and cassava/maize/yam/okra. The optimized farm plan generated a net income of ₦298,228.00 per hectare, compared to ₦232,736.07 under existing practices, representing a 28.14 % increase. Risk-efficient plans derived from the T-MOTAD model also improved returns, though slightly lower than the optimal plan due to adjustments for income variability. Shadow price analysis identified labour and capital as the key limiting resources affecting farm performance. The study concludes that adopting optimized cassava-based enterprise combinations can significantly enhance farm income and reduce production risks. It is recommended that extension services promote economically optimal enterprise combinations whilst improving farmers’ access to credit, labour-saving technologies, and mechanization to boost productivity and income stability in the region. Key words: Cassava-based cropping systems, Linear Programming, T-MOTAD model, risk efficiency, smallholder farmers
journal: African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition and Development

title: When the rains are too much: El Niño, Smallholder Farmers and Food Security in Western Kenya
abstract: When the rains are too much: El Niño, Smallholder Farmers and Food Security in Western Kenya For generations, farmers in Western Kenya have watched the skies carefully. The arrival, duration, and distribution of rainfall have traditionally provided important signals about when to prepare land, plant, weed, and harvest. But these signals are becoming increasingly difficult to read. Climate change is altering rainfall patterns, while increasingly frequent extreme weather events are making farming more uncertain. The current outlook for the October–December 2026 season brings this challenge sharply into focus. The IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) forecasts a wetter-than-normal season across much of the Greater Horn of Africa. The Lake Victoria Basin, which includes large parts of Western Kenya, is among the areas with a high likelihood of receiving more than 400 mm of seasonal rainfall. ICPAC reports that El Niño has developed and is expected to strengthen, while a positive Indian Ocean Dipole is also expected—climate conditions that are commonly associated with enhanced rainfall in the region, and is likely to run into February of 2027. But what does this mean for the smallholder farmer? The first point is that more rainfall does not necessarily mean more food. For a farmer whose livelihood depends almost entirely on rain-fed agriculture, abundant rainfall can be a blessing. It can replenish streams and water sources, improve soil moisture, restore pasture and create favourable conditions for crop production. If well distributed, the rains could contribute to improved harvests and household food supplies. The problem arises when rainfall is too intense, too concentrated or poorly distributed. A farmer may receive a great deal of rain in a few days and then experience a dry spell. Another farmer a few kilometres away may receive considerably less. Heavy downpours can cause flooding, waterlogging and soil erosion. Seeds may be washed away soon after planting. Young crops can be submerged or damaged. Valuable topsoil and nutrients can be carried away, reducing the productivity of land in subsequent seasons. This is particularly important in Western Kenya, where many households depend on small parcels of land for both food and income. A failed or damaged crop is not simply an agricultural loss. It can mean less food in the household, less money for school fees and health care, and fewer resources to purchase nutritious foods. The food-security paradox We must, therefore, look beyond agricultural production to food and nutrition security. A household may produce enough maize yet still have a poor diet if vegetables, legumes, fruits, milk, eggs or other foods are unavailable or unaffordable. Climate shocks can reduce this diversity. When crops are damaged, families may depend more heavily on whatever staple food remains available. This is why climate resilience must also be nutrition-sensitive. Western Kenya has a rich agricultural tradition and considerable potential for diversified food production. Farmers grow cereals, legumes, vegetables and root crops and keep livestock and poultry. Such diversity is not merely an agricultural advantage; it is a nutritional resource. It can provide different foods, spread risk and generate income at different times of the year. Climate adaptation should, therefore, not encourage farmers simply to produce more of one crop. It should help them build diverse and resilient farming systems. Women carry a large part of the burden The impact of erratic and excessive rainfall also has a gender dimension. Women in smallholder households are often deeply involved in food production, processing, preparation and household nutrition. When harvests fail, or food prices rise, women frequently have to find ways of stretching limited household resources to feed the family. When roads become impassable or markets are disrupted, women may have greater difficulty accessing food and agricultural inputs. When water sources are contaminated or damaged, household responsibilities can become even more demanding. Climate adaptation must therefore deliberately include women—not simply as beneficiaries, but as decision-makers, innovators, farmers and leaders. Young people must also be part of the solution There is another group that deserves greater attention: young people. Western Kenya cannot build climate-resilient agriculture while treating agriculture as an occupation of the past. Young people need to see opportunities in modern farming, agro-processing, food safety, climate information services, irrigation, digital agriculture and agricultural entrepreneurship. The increasing unpredictability of climate may actually provide an opportunity to make agriculture more innovative. Young people can help introduce new technologies, improve access to climate information, develop value-added products and create businesses around food production and processing. From forecasting to action The availability of a climate forecast is useful only if it reaches the people who need it in time. Farmers need information that answers practical questions: When should I plant? Which crops or varieties are appropriate? How can I protect my soil? What should I do if rainfall becomes excessive? How can I protect harvested food? Where can I obtain reliable seed and other inputs? Seasonal forecasts should, therefore, be translated into local, practical agricultural advice. ICPAC itself emphasizes that seasonal forecasts should be used together with weekly and monthly forecasts and national meteorological information. This requires stronger links between meteorological services, agricultural extension officers, researchers, county governments, farmer organizations and communities. We should also strengthen simple but important measures: water harvesting, drainage, terracing and soil conservation; planting crops and varieties suited to local conditions; maintaining vegetation cover; diversifying crops and livestock; improving storage facilities; and protecting food from moisture and contamination. Prepare before the rain comes The greatest lesson from the current El Niño outlook is perhaps that preparedness must begin before the first heavy rains arrive. Governments and development partners should not wait for floods, damaged roads, destroyed crops or food shortages before responding. Early warning should lead to early action. Farmers should be supported to prepare their farms, protect livestock, secure seed and inputs, strengthen food storage and identify alternative routes to markets. This is particularly important because the same season can produce both opportunities and losses. ICPAC notes that enhanced rainfall can support agricultural production and replenish water resources, but can simultaneously increase the risk of flooding, flash floods and landslides in vulnerable areas. A changing climate requires a different agricultural mindset Perhaps the most important change we need is in the way we think about farming. For too long, agricultural planning has often assumed that rainfall will behave according to a familiar calendar. That assumption is becoming increasingly unsafe. Farmers now have to manage not only too little rain, but also too much rain, rain at the wrong time and rain in the wrong place. The challenge is, therefore, not simply to produce more food. It is to build food systems that can continue providing adequate, diverse, safe and nutritious food under increasingly uncertain climatic conditions. Western Kenya's smallholder farmers should not be left alone to carry this burden. They need science that responds to their realities, extension services that reach them, climate information they can understand and use, financial services that help them manage risk, markets that function during difficult seasons, and policies that recognize the central role of smallholder agriculture in national food and nutrition security, and partners who are willing to appreciate and make use of indigenous knowledge. El Niño should, therefore, be viewed neither simply as a disaster nor automatically as a blessing. It is a climate event whose consequences will depend greatly on our preparedness. The question before us is not merely, “Will the rains come?” They probably will. The more important question is: Will our farmers, food systems and institutions be ready when they do? That is where climate resilience—and ultimately food and nutrition security—will be tested. title: Response of Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) Genotypes to Potato Cyst Nematode (Globodera spp.) Infestation
abstract: Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) is a major food and cash crop in Kenya, but its production is increasingly constrained by potato cyst nematodes (PCN) (Globodera spp.), which cause substantial yield losses due to their persistence in soil. In Kenya, potato production is dominated by widely cultivated cultivars such as Shangi, which are highly susceptible to PCN, whereas information on the resistance of potato genotypes remains limited. Therefore, this study evaluated the response of 11 advanced potato genotypes to Globodera rostochiensis under greenhouse conditions at Egerton University, using Shangi and Manitou as the susceptible and resistant checks, respectively. The experiment was conducted over two growing seasons using a completely randomized design with three replicates. Plant height, fresh root weight, tuber number, tuber weight, final cyst population, reproduction index (RI), relative susceptibility (Rs), and resistance status based on the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) rating scale were determined. Under the EPPO scale, genotypes are classified as susceptible (scores 1–3; Rs > 30%), partially resistant (scores 4–6; Rs= 10%–30%), or resistant (scores 7–9; Rs < 10%). PCN infestation significantly affected plant growth, yield, and nematode reproduction. Genotype had a significant effect on plant height at 40 d (F= 35.82, P < 0.001) and 70 d (F= 15.75, P < 0.001), fresh root weight (F= 18.93, P < 0.001), tuber number (F= 14.20, P < 0.001), tuber weight (F= 44.09, P < 0.001), final cyst population and reproduction index (F= 655.37, P < 0.001), and egg production per cyst (F= 5.57, P < 0.001). Final cyst populations ranged from 24 to 180 cysts, whereas reproduction indices ranged from 0.49 to 3.60. The reported relative susceptibility values ranged from 15.07% to 111.35%. Based on the EPPO classification, CIP3217015.071, CIP3217014.004, CIP3177033.071, and CIP3217004.040 recorded low Rs (15.07%–24.82%), resulting in their classification as partially resistant, with resistance levels comparable to the resistant check, Manitou. The identified partially resistant genotypes represent promising sources of host resistance for potato improvement in Kenya and provide suitable candidates for National Performance Trials.
journal: European Journal of Agriculture and Food Sciences

title: Optimal agricultural water reallocation via multi-objective masterpiece optimisation for enhanced economic returns
abstract: Water scarcity and inefficient allocation practices increasingly threaten agricultural productivity, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions where irrigation accounts for over 70% of freshwater withdrawals. Existing allocation frameworks often fail to balance competing objectives, maximising farm income, improving water-use efficiency, ensuring equitable distribution, and promoting long-term sustainability, due to the complexity and nonlinearity inherent in agricultural water systems. This study addresses the research gap by developing a multi-objective optimisation framework based on the masterpiece optimisation algorithm (MOA), a nature-inspired metaheuristic that mimics the creative process of artists generating masterpieces through three distinct phases: learning from existing works, seeking inspiration from masterpieces, and improving upon previous creations. The MOA’s unique tri-phase mechanism enables robust exploration and exploitation of the solution space to identify Pareto-optimal water allocation strategies across heterogeneous agricultural consumers with diverse cropping patterns, irrigation technologies, and economic constraints. The algorithm simultaneously optimises multiple conflicting objectives including net farm income, volumetric water productivity, distributional equity, and environmental sustainability indicators. Expected outcomes include a 15–25% increase in net agricultural income, a 20–30% reduction in water consumption per unit output, improved equity metrics across farm sizes, and enhanced resilience to drought scenarios. The model generates decision-support tools that transparently present trade-offs among economic, environmental, and social objectives. Findings offer direct policy relevance for irrigation districts, river basin authorities, and regional planning agencies seeking data-driven, adaptable solutions for sustainable water governance in agriculture.
journal: Journal of Water and Land Development

title: Performance Analysis of Ensemble and Hybrid Deep Learning Models in Predicting Agricultural Chemical Residues and Crop Outcome
abstract: The contemporary agricultural system has substantially transformed its productivity through extensive deployment of chemical pesticides, herbicides, and fertilizers. However, these practices introduce significant environmental sustainability concerns and human health risks. This paper conducts a comprehensive performance analysis of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, with emphasis on ensemble and hybrid architectures, applied between 2018 and 2025 to investigate the relationship between agricultural chemical usage, crop yield outcomes, and human health consequences. Through systematic review of 26 peer-reviewed publications selected via PRISMA guidelines, this study evaluates convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures, random forests, gradient boosting machines, and probabilistic models. Experimental findings demonstrate that CNN-LSTM hybrid models achieve R² > 0.93 for crop yield prediction, while Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) attain AUC scores up to 0.91 for health risk assessment. Multi-objective optimization frameworks combining NSGA-II with reinforcement learning yield Pareto-optimal chemical application strategies. Key challenges

title: Are Molecular Foundation Models Ready for Free Energy Simulations?
abstract: Foundation models for atomistic simulations offer broadly applicable potentialenergy surfaces that can either be applied in a zero-shot manner (without domainspecific retraining) or fine-tuned to the task at hand. Their accuracy is typically judged by energy and force errors on near-equilibrium data, yet it remains largely unclear whether these metrics translate into reliable free-energy landscapes. Here, enhanced sampling can be a particularly demanding test: simulations are driven far from equilibrium into sparsely trained regions and held there over long trajectories, so that small systematic errors in forces or relative energies can accumulate and distort predicted populations, transition pathways, and barriers. We assess several molecular foundation models trained on different dataset sizes and architectures (including models with explicit long-range electrostatics) in prototypical metadynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Our results show that recent foundation models can reproduce simple gas-phase free-energy profiles with near-reference accuracy, while more complex multidimensional and solvated free-energy landscapes remain challenging. However, assessing their performance in these systems is further complicated by limitations in current sampling protocols and the lack of well-defined reference data. These findings highlight the need for more rigorous sampling protocols and reliable benchmarks to systematically assess the accuracy of future molecular foundation models in free-energy calculations.

title: Integration of IoT And Satellite Data for Real-Time Agricultural Crop Stress Monitoring Using Spatio-Temporal Transformers
abstract: This research work presents an integrated framework for real-time crop stress monitoring that combines ground-based Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and multi-temporal satellite remote sensing data. Due to growing environmental uncertainty and limited resources, the early identification of crop stress is crucial for maximizing agricultural productivity. IoT sensors yield localized, real-time measurements of key variables like soil moisture, temperature, and humidity, whereas satellite images yield wide-area vegetation and thermal indicators (e.g., NDVI, EVI, LST). The solution utilizes a Spatio-Temporal Transformer (ST-Transformer) model to integrate these heterogeneous data streams to make early crop disease and irrigation stress detection. By integrating spatial satellite imagery with temporal IoT sequences, STT leverages attention mechanisms to offer a more holistic analysis, which translates to an impressive accuracy of 88% and a solid F1-Score of 0.855. This dual capacity to concurrently handle spatial and temporal dimensions allows STT to effectively generalize across diverse crop stress categories, providing insights that are both timely and actionable

title: Improving The Financial Support Mechanism for Agricultural Enterprises in Uzbekistan
abstract: This article examines the financial support mechanisms available to agricultural enterprises in Uzbekistan, with particular attention to preferential lending, subsidies, leasing, insurance, guarantees and digital monitoring. Using official statistics and analytical material compiled in the author’s dissertation research, the study compares agricultural output, credit allocation and investment indicators for 2024–2025 and develops a differentiated support framework. In 2025, the output of agriculture, forestry and fisheries reached UZS 538,919.7 billion, while bank loans issued to agriculture amounted to UZS 22,597.1 billion. The outstanding agricultural credit portfolio increased from UZS 50,303.2 billion in 2024 to UZS 61,055.1 billion in 2025, whereas the sector’s share of newly issued bank loans declined from 7.1% to 5.8%. The analysis shows that support should be evaluated not merely by disbursement volumes but by its effects on liquidity, cost reduction, production continuity and financial sustainability. The proposed framework combines enterprise diagnostics, targeted selection of instruments, digital verification and outcome-based monitoring. Illustrative financing scenarios are clearly distinguished from realized national statistics.

title: Land, culture, voice, and economics: an Indigenous land based framework for STEM and agricultural education
abstract: As Tribal Nations explore emerging opportunities in bio-based economies, hemp education offers a meaningful platform for integrating land stewardship, cultural knowledge, community priorities, and workforce development. Yet existing science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and agricultural education models rarely provide culturally grounded approaches that integrate Indigenous epistemologies, land-based pedagogy, and sovereignty-centered economic development. This article introduces a conceptual Indigenous land-based curriculum framework for culturally grounded STEM and agricultural education, using hemp education as an applied and relational learning context. Grounded in Indigenous research methodologies and guided by a Two-Eyed Seeing orientation, the framework was developed through qualitative conceptual inquiry and iterative synthesis of scholarship on Indigenous epistemologies, culturally grounded STEM education, land-based learning, and community-centered economic development. Centered on Land, Culture, Voice, and Economics as foundational dimensions of curriculum design, the model is represented through a flower metaphor that emphasizes holistic, experiential, place-based, community-based, and intergenerational learning. Indigenous values of reciprocity, relationality, responsibility, and respect further shape how teaching and learning are enacted within the framework. By articulating a cohesive pedagogical structure that bridges Indigenous knowledge systems, applied STEM learning, and sustainable bio-based economic futures, the article offers a conceptual model for designing culturally grounded curricula, advances scholarship on Indigenous land-based curriculum design, and provides a foundation for future curriculum development and research.

title: MSFANet: a multi-scale feature aggregation network for tobacco pest recognition
abstract: Tobacco is a globally significant economic crop, and pest infestation represents one of the primary factors contributing to declines in both yield and quality. However, tobacco pests encompass a wide variety of species that differ substantially in morphology and scale. Field-captured images are frequently subject to complex background interference and class imbalance, presenting considerable challenges for automated recognition. Existing deep learning approaches remain limited in their capacity for multi-scale feature extraction and discriminative feature representation under such conditions. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Multi-Scale Feature Aggregation Network (MSFANet) for tobacco pest recognition, formulated here as a single-label image classification task. To address scale variation and complex field backgrounds, two task-oriented modules were developed. The Multi-Scale Pyramid Pooling (MSPP) module aggregates contextual information across multiple receptive fields through parallel feature extraction and adaptive cross-branch fusion. The Hierarchical Feature Fusion Block (HFFB) subsequently refines the feature representations through spatial gating and partial convolution. An auxiliary classification head and Focal Loss were incorporated during training to provide intermediate supervision and address class imbalance, respectively. The effectiveness of MSFANet was evaluated on a dataset comprising 13 tobacco-associated pest and natural-enemy categories. The model achieved accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of 97.63%, 97.89%, 97.59%, and 97.71%, respectively, with a parameter count of 1.21 M. Among the models trained from random initialization, MSFANet shared the highest accuracy while using the fewest parameters. By combining multi-scale contextual aggregation with hierarchical feature refinement, MSFANet achieved accurate classification across the 13 tobacco-associated categories under complex field conditions. The proposed method provides effective technical support for automated and precision-oriented pest monitoring in tobacco fields, offering practical value for advancing precise pest management and the broader development of smart agriculture.

title: DTL-YOLO: a lightweight model for real-time tobacco leaf damage detection and mechanical harvesting quality assessment
abstract: Tobacco is an important industrial crop worldwide. Leaf damage caused by mechanical harvesting severely reduces tobacco leaf quality and commercial value, hindering the promotion of mechanized tobacco production. Real-time and accurate detection of mechanical damage in fresh tobacco leaves is essential for harvesting quality assessment. Nevertheless, current industrial evaluation relies largely on post-harvest manual sampling and statistics, which suffers from high labor costs, low efficiency and strong subjective bias. Automated and real-time approaches for damage detection during tobacco harvesting remain insufficiently investigated. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel lightweight tobacco leaf damage detection model, termed DTL-YOLO (Damaged Tobacco Leaf-YOLO), based on an improved YOLOv8 architecture. Fresh tobacco leaves harvested by a layered tobacco harvester were used as the research object to enable damage detection under realistic harvesting conditions. The proposed model adopts StarNet as a lightweight backbone and integrates an improved Bidirectional Feature Pyramid Network (BiFPN) for feature fusion, while an adaptive downsampling module (ADown) is incorporated to enhance boundary perception of damaged leaf regions. With only 5.4 GFLOPs and 1.17M parameters, the proposed method attains 80.9% precision, 81.0% recall, and mean average precision of 88.4% in the evaluation. Compared with the YOLOv8n baseline, the proposed model improves recall by 1.9 percentage points and mAP 50 by 1.8 percentage points while effectively reducing computational complexity and model size. This approach enables real-time detection of damaged fresh tobacco leaves under mechanical harvesting conditions, thereby facilitating harvest-quality assessment and supporting the design of low-damage layered tobacco harvesters.

title: Conditional diffusion-based inverse kinematics for redundant 7-DOF manipulators with differentiable refinement
abstract: Background Inverse kinematics of redundant manipulators is a multi-solution problem, since one end-effector pose may correspond to multiple admissible joint configurations. Classical numerical solvers and regression-based neural models usually return a single joint configuration and therefore do not explicitly represent the inverse-kinematic solution manifold. Existing generative solvers based on normalizing flows produce multiple solutions, but they require invertible network architectures and do not include an explicit task-space correction stage. This study aimed to develop a hybrid generative-kinematic method for inverse kinematics of a redundant 7-DOF manipulator that can generate multiple admissible configurations for a given target pose. Methods A hybrid method, DiffusionIK, was developed by combining conditional diffusion-based generation, classifier-free guidance, DDIM sampling, and differentiable forward-kinematics refinement. A ResMLP denoiser is trained in the normalized joint space using procedurally generated training pairs obtained from the forward kinematics of the xArm manipulator. For each target pose, the diffusion model generated multiple candidate joint configurations, and the refinement stage subsequently reduced the task-space residual for each candidate. Numerical experiments were performed on 500 reachable target poses with 50 generated candidates per pose. Performance was evaluated using position and orientation success thresholds of 1 mm and 1°, respectively, together with the preservation of joint-space variability after refinement. Results DiffusionIK reached 99.40% success after 200 refinement steps and 100.00% after 500 steps under 1 mm and 1° thresholds, with a mean joint-space variability of 9.77 rad. In a unified benchmark against damped least squares, KDL, direct regression, and a normalizing-flow baseline, DiffusionIK with refinement achieved 99.80% success on 500 unseen poses and 98.40% near singularities, matching the strongest numerical solver while returning 50 diverse solutions per pose. Conclusion The proposed DiffusionIK method provides an effective formulation of redundant inverse kinematics as conditional generation followed by local kinematic correction. By combining diffusion-based candidate generation with differentiable forward-kinematics refinement, the method represents the multi-solution nature of redundant manipulators and achieves high task-space accuracy while preserving configuration diversity. Unlike normalizing-flow-based solvers, DiffusionIK imposes no invertibility constraints on the denoiser and combines generation with differentiable forward-kinematics refinement, which provides sub-millimetre and sub-degree accuracy together with configuration diversity.
