title: From Linear Regression to Temporal Fusion Transformers: Benchmarking Electricity Price Forecasting Models in Markets with Different Renewable Energy Shares
abstract: Rising renewable penetration increases wholesale price volatility and challenges traditional forecasting approaches. This paper benchmarks three methods—adaptive linear regression, Random Forest (RF), and the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)—on hourly day-ahead prices in four European markets with contrasting generation mixes: Slovakia (nuclear-dominated), Spain (solar-rich), Denmark (wind-dominated), and Germany (mixed). Using Energy-Charts data for 2015–2025, all the models are evaluated under one day-ahead protocol on a common 12-month hold-out against naive 24-h persistence. With price-history features, the RF significantly outperforms persistence in three of four markets. A single cross-market five-seed TFT ensemble attains the lowest MAE everywhere, cutting the persistence error by 55.6% in Germany (to 12.88 €/MWh) and 21.7% in Slovakia. The improvement is generally larger in markets with higher variable-renewable penetration, though not strictly monotonic. Replacing the realized fundamentals with TSO day-ahead forecasts changes the MAE by at most 0.22 €/MWh: the day-ahead price is itself formed from those forecasts. Multivariate Diebold–Mariano tests confirm both advantages everywhere on absolute errors. Quantile averaging yields pinball losses of 3.87–6.53 €/MWh, but the 80% intervals cover only 71–78%. Variable importance ties the leading driver to each mix: wind in Denmark and Germany, load and solar in Spain, and load in Slovakia.

title: Fruit Quality Classification Through Feature Fusion and Deep Learning
abstract: Fruit quality assessment is an integral part of food safety, loss reduction after harvest and consumer satisfaction. In modern agricultural production systems, where quality control is essential for ensuring both domestic and export markets, it continues to play a vital role. Manual grading, which is widely used, is poorly time-efficient, imprecise, and prone to human error, and is reliant upon the human eye and human skill. Such limiting practices can result in variability and, in large-scale production, high operating expenses. In this paper, we propose a hybrid classification model using deep learning features extracted from ResNet50V2 along with traditional handcrafted features such as Histogram of Gradients (HOG), Local Binary Patterns (LBP), and color, texture and shape descriptors. The purpose of this study is to develop a model to combine high-level and low-level feature representation to gain a comprehensive understanding of fruit quality characteristics. The proposed preprocessing technique will be followed by data augmentation, ANOVA-based feature selection, and classification using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). This multi-stage course of action is specifically designed so that the extracted features are appropriate, relevant and discriminative for correct classification. For experimentation, standard datasets were chosen as FruitNet and tomato. There are six fruit types included in the FruitNet dataset with three different quality classes, and another tomato dataset with three ripeness-based classes. XGBoost always outperforms other classifiers on the FruitNet dataset with an accuracy of 97.3% and on the tomato dataset with an accuracy of 92%. The findings validate the validity of the proposed model and its use in all crops under all grading systems.

title: Applications and Future Prospects of Plant Multi-Omics Technologies in Precision Agriculture
abstract: Against the backdrop of global population growth, intensifying climate change, and limited arable land, ensuring food security and promoting sustainable agriculture have become critical issues. The limitations of conventional agricultural systems are becoming increasingly apparent, creating an urgent need for innovation driven by science and technology. In this context, plant multi-omics technologies serve as the foundational data and technical cornerstone of systems biology and precision agriculture. Integrating multi-level data from genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, epigenomics, and microbiomics offers substantial advantages for systematically understanding and improving plants. Unlike previous reviews that mainly catalog omics technologies or focus on individual crops, this review adopts a unified discovery-to-translation framework and critically evaluates the strength of evidence across applications. This review focuses on cutting-edge applications of multi-omics in three key areas: improving the traits of cereal crops (rice, wheat and maize), remediating soil health, and innovating products such as biofertilizers and biostimulants for agriculture. We systematically explore the roles of multi-omics in accelerating breeding processes, deciphering complex agronomic traits, restoring soil ecosystems, and constructing intelligent decision-support systems. The review also examines current challenges, including the complexity of data integration and the difficulties of predicting genotype-by-environment interactions. Furthermore, it outlines future directions involving deeper convergence with artificial intelligence, high-throughput phenomics, and digital twins. In summary, plant multi-omics technology is a vital tool for unravelling the mysteries of plant life and is also a key enabler of intelligent, precise and sustainable agricultural transformation.

title: Biodegradable Nanoclay–Agarose Hydrogels as Sustainable Substrates for Seed Germination
abstract: Conventional seedling substrates such as rockwool and peat raise environmental concerns associated with disposal and resource extraction. Here, we investigate nanoclay–agarose hydrogels as candidate sustainable and biodegradable alternatives for seed germination and early plant growth under greenhouse conditions. Agarose hydrogels incorporating sodium bentonite nanoclay (NC) or activated carbon (AC) were prepared and evaluated for their structural, thermal, and biological performance using Brassica rapa (bok choy) as a model crop. Structural and physicochemical analyses revealed lamellar architectures, spectral features consistent with agarose–filler interactions, and composition-dependent thermal decomposition profiles. Dried NC hydrogels exhibited more open structures than the comparatively compact AC hydrogels. After 15 days under greenhouse conditions, NC40 (40 wt% nanoclay relative to agarose) achieved 100% germination and the highest mean fresh and dry biomass among the substrates compared for biomass, including rockwool and peat pellets. Over 42 days of soil burial, pure agarose and AC hydrogels showed more extensive visible breakdown consistent with biodegradation of the agarose matrix, whereas NC hydrogels retained their structural form for longer. These findings highlight nanoclay–agarose hydrogels as biodegradable, eco-engineered substrates with the potential to replace conventional growing media and advance sustainable agriculture.

title: Improved Pointwise Ensemble Surrogate Modelling for Assembly Deviation Analysis of Thin-Walled Parts
abstract: For assembly deviation analysis of thin-walled parts, single surrogate models are suitable for cases with simple assembly processes and few design variables. For complex parts with high flexibility, nonlinear behavior, and variable spring-back effects, ensemble surrogate models are more suitable. To address the deficiencies of the existing Pointwise Ensemble with Adaptive Function and Heuristic Formulation (PEAH) in terms of the continuity of the weight function and local adaptability, this paper proposes an improved kernel-weighted method, denoted as KW-PEAH. Specifically, it introduces a Gaussian kernel function to replace linear distance weighting for smooth distance decay, and employs a K-nearest neighbor (KNN) strategy to dynamically adjust the kernel bandwidth based on local sample density. KW-PEAH was compared with four ensemble methods and the original PEAH, using eight benchmark functions and a simulation-based thin-walled assembly case under noise. Compared with the PEAH method, the NRMSE values on the BH and ER functions are reduced by approximately 6.2% and 2.9%, respectively. In the simulation-based thin-walled assembly case, KW-PEAH achieves lower RMSE and MAE and higher mean R2 at all three noise levels. Under the 10% noise level, the mean RMSE and MAE are reduced by approximately 6.7% and 5.6%. Overall, the results indicate that KW-PEAH is suited for thin-walled part deviation analysis in low- to medium-dimensional, noisy scenarios.

title: Moral Judgment Without Moral Agency: Why Judgment Accuracy Does Not Ground Moral Agency in the Age of AI
abstract: As large language models increasingly match human performance on moral-judgment tasks, two bodies of literature have developed in parallel. Empirical moral psychology treats moral judgment as an output and benchmarks artificial systems against human responses. The philosophy of artificial moral agency denies agency to such systems mainly on the ground of sentience, an empirically inaccessible criterion that has left the debate stalled. This paper argues that human–AI convergence in moral judgment conceals a categorical asymmetry that neither literature has theorized. Drawing on Spinoza’s conatus and Damasio’s account of homeostasis and affect, it argues that moral agency presupposes affective-homeostatic self-maintenance as its constitutive ground: the organization from which valuation first arises. This condition is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim is constitutive rather than normative, so it does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” Sentience is repositioned as the experiential manifestation of this organization rather than the explanatory terminus. Contemporary AI systems, including those trained with human feedback, are therefore moral judges without moral agency. The paper closes with a behavioral research program, including concrete experimental designs, on the conditions under which people attribute moral agency to human and artificial agents.

title: Field-Informed Prediction of Sand Erosion and Dynamic Risk Assessment for Tight-Gas Pipelines in a Gathering Station
abstract: Sand production and proppant flowback in tight-gas reservoirs introduce gas–liquid–sand three-phase flow into wellbore and surface gathering systems, where particle-laden streams simultaneously cause mechanical erosion, electrochemical corrosion, and their synergistic wall-thickness loss at bends, tees, chokes, and separators. This study develops a novel field-informed prediction framework that, for the first time, couples gas–liquid–sand three-phase flow, orientation-dependent sand transport probability (STP), erosion–corrosion models with multi-size particle superposition, and Bow-Tie/Bayesian-network-based dynamic risk assessment into a single operating-envelope calculation. The key innovations include: (i) a unified erosion–corrosion coupling model that integrates mechanical erosion, electrochemical CO2 corrosion, and their synergistic interaction through particle-size-distribution-weighted superposition; (ii) a four-pipeline-type differentiation (inlet, gas outlet, sand outlet, water outlet) revealing that erosion–corrosion severity varies by more than a factor of three among pipeline types; and (iii) a Poisson–Gamma dynamic risk updating model that tracks failure probability evolution under time-varying operating conditions. The framework was applied to three tight-gas wells and their gathering pipeline network. Field sieve analysis constrained particle-size distributions (70–160 mesh), and the sand samples were confirmed as quartz-rich proppant (Mohs hardness 7) based on sieve analysis and visual inspection. Horizontal-section STP ranged from 76.25% to 91.43%, and vertical-section STP reached 100% in all wells. The predicted erosion–corrosion rate for the KQ51H pipeline was 1.866 mm/a, exceeding the critical threshold and classifying it as High risk. Model predictions of wall-thickness loss at 11 monitoring locations agreed with ultrasonic thickness measurements within 10% error. The Bow-Tie model identified sand mass rate, particle-size distribution, and corrosion-product film failure as critical risk drivers. Dynamic Bayesian updating tracked failure probability evolution over 12 months, with the highest-risk segment showing a probability increase from 0.0149 to 0.0325. The framework supports differentiated inspection scheduling and mitigation prioritization across pipeline segments in a gathering station.

title: Cross-Field Transfer of UAV-Based Winter Wheat Yield Prediction: Model Transferability and Sample Efficiency
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) remote sensing is widely used for plot-scale crop yield prediction, but model performance may decline when models are transferred across fields with different crop, environmental, management, and sensing conditions. This study evaluated the cross-field transferability of UAV-based winter wheat yield models using multispectral (MS), RGB, and thermal infrared (TIR) information. Categorical Boosting (CatBoost) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models were evaluated under five strategies: target-only training (T1), direct transfer (T2), nitrogen-based adaptation (T3), cultivar-based adaptation (T4), and mixed adaptation (T5). Direct transfer increased the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) from 12.7% to 14.0% for CatBoost and from 12.9% to 15.9% for MLP. Mixed adaptation achieved the best overall performance, with coefficient of determination (R2) values of 0.84 and 0.87 and NRMSE values of 11.7% and 10.9% for CatBoost and MLP, respectively. After controlling for calibration sample size, the difference between T3 and T4 became smaller, indicating that adaptation performance was influenced by both calibration-data composition and sample availability. CatBoost showed diminishing returns near the 40% calibration level in this experiment, whereas MLP continued to benefit from additional target-domain samples. Prediction errors were higher for samples beyond the source-domain yield range, while mixed adaptation reduced prediction errors in both yield-range groups. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and sensor-level ablation showed that MS features provided important predictive information, while RGB and TIR provided complementary information. These results indicate that target-domain adaptation can improve cross-field UAV yield prediction and highlight the importance of calibration design, yield-range mismatch, and multi-sensor information when transferring models to new fields.

title: APFNet: An Adaptive Perception Fusion Network for Multi-Scale Object Detection in Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate multi-scale object detection remains challenging in remote sensing (RS) imagery due to severe scale variation, limited pixel occupancy of small targets, and complex backgrounds. Existing multi-scale fusion methods propagate features along predefined cross-scale paths and apply receptive fields fixed once trained, so fusion weights and the spatial range of contextual evidence remain largely input-independent. The Adaptive Perception Fusion Network (APFNet) targets these two aspects through four operations: (1) Split-ELAN (SP-ELAN), a channel-compressed serial refinement backbone whose design is motivated by small-object feature preservation; (2) Adaptive Sampling (AS), which produces sample-dependent channel weights from a global descriptor during cross-scale alignment; (3) Adaptive Gating (AG), which is coupled with AS and aggregates the recalibrated features at complementary receptive-field scales; and (4) Adaptive Context Aggregation (ACA), which aligns three feature levels and applies parallel large-kernel depthwise branches to supply broader multi-scale context. On DIOR, APFNet-L achieves three-run mean values of 86.39% AP50, 63.09% AP, and 26.10% APS. A complete 23 component-group study under one scratch/no-augmentation protocol yields positive conditional contrasts for SP-ELAN, ACA, and the coupled AS–AG pathway. LEVIR and RSOD provide additional cross-dataset and configuration-selection results. These operations use established primitives; the contribution lies in their routing and aggregation.

title: Effect of Sun Glints from Ice Clouds on MODIS Data Products
abstract: This paper examines the way sun glints from horizontally oriented ice crystals that occur in clouds impact atmospheric data products provided by the Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS). For this, the paper presents a statistical analysis of two years of MODIS data from all tropical land regions. The results indicate only weak glint effects on cloud amount and height, as these values are obtained using mainly observations of (inherently glint-free) thermal infrared radiation. In contrast, glints are found to cause a roughly 10% increase in mean retrieved cloud optical thickness, and 10% decreases in mean particle size and in the prevalence of ice cloud phase. Moreover, glints from undetected ice clouds are found to cause roughly 5% increases in mean aerosol optical depth and coarse mode fraction, and positive and negative biases comparable to the magnitude of the seasonal cycle in total column ozone and precipitable water vapor amounts, respectively. Given the modest size of glints, the effects are most important to consider in studies that use data from a limited range of viewing zenith angles (e.g., around nadir). The results are relevant to MODIS and to other satellite imagers that use similar retrieval algorithms, and thus likely experience similar glint effects.

title: Multi-Index Remote Sensing Assessment of Agro-Climatic Change and Agricultural Responses in Temperate and Semi-Arid Regions
abstract: Diverse climatic regions exhibit unique agro-climatic vulnerabilities that are significantly shaped by climate stress. Understanding these distinct vulnerabilities is essential for developing effective policies to mitigate climate change impacts and ensuring sustainable environmental management. This study examines agro-climatic vulnerabilities in Nottinghamshire County (United Kingdom) and Udaipur District (India) from 2000 to 2024, comparing climate change impacts across temperate and semi-arid agricultural systems that represent fundamentally different system behaviours under contrasting climatic conditions. Using multi-temporal Landsat imagery and WorldClim climate data, nine environmental indices were analysed: the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), Moisture Stress Index (MSI), Land Surface Temperature (LST), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Health Index (VHI), Drought Risk Index (DRI), and Crop Health Index (CHI). The results reveal contrasting regional trajectories that challenge conventional assumptions about climate vulnerability. Udaipur exhibited improved vegetation and moisture conditions across the observation period, whereas Nottinghamshire showed intensifying moisture stress and declining precipitation. Warming was more pronounced in Nottinghamshire, while strong inter-index correlations validated the monitoring approach. These findings indicate that Udaipur benefits from intensified monsoon patterns, requiring flood mitigation and water-storage infrastructure, whereas Nottinghamshire’s rising moisture stress underscores the need for sustained monitoring and adaptive management. This comparative framework provides evidence-based insights for region-specific adaptation strategies essential to sustainable agricultural development across diverse agro-climatic zones.
